vocab.means: A story told to entertain, with characters, a setting and a problem. A recipe is not a narrative.
The start of a story: who, where, when and a hint of trouble. It is not the ending.
The problem the characters must try to solve. Without it, nothing exciting happens.
The ending, where the problem is solved or wrapped up. A cliffhanger leaves it open.
How an author shows what a character is like through looks, actions, words and thoughts.
What a character is like inside, such as brave or greedy. Tall is how they look, not a trait.
Where and when a story happens. A character's name is not part of the setting.
The worried, edge-of-your-seat feeling when something might go wrong. A calm picnic has none.
A word that describes, counts or groups a noun: muddy, three, pumpkin. Run is a verb, not an adjective.
A group of words telling when, where, how or why: behind the shed. It is not a sentence on its own.
A doing word you can see or hear: crept, leapt, slammed. Was and is are not action verbs.
A sentence that states a fact or opinion and ends with a full stop. A question is not declarative.
A sentence that shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark: What a feast!
Two ideas that could each stand alone, joined by and, but or so. A list of words is not one.
A joining word such as and, but or so. It links ideas in a sentence.
A new story that carries on from an earlier one. A retell of the same story is not a sequel.

misconceptions.think: An orientation just tells us the characters' names.
misconceptions.fix: Use the Orientation planner: who, where, when, a hint of the problem and an engaging detail. Check each box against the opening of the mentor text.

misconceptions.think: More adjectives always make writing better.
misconceptions.fix: Show the too little, too much and just right sentences from Lesson 10. Aim for one or two precise adjectives per noun.

misconceptions.think: A character trait is what a character looks like.
misconceptions.fix: Sort words into inside (traits) and outside (looks). Ask: what does the character do that shows this?

misconceptions.think: Any two sentences joined with and make a good compound sentence.
misconceptions.fix: Teach but for contrast and so for result. Students test: does each part make sense alone, and does the joining word match the meaning?

misconceptions.think: You build tension by saying something is scary.
misconceptions.fix: Show, don't tell: break the moment into small steps, use strong verbs and sounds, and let the reader feel it.

misconceptions.think: To add a suffix you just stick it on the end.
misconceptions.fix: Teach the checks: drop the e (chase, chasing), change y to i after a consonant (berry, berries), keep y after a vowel (play, played), double after a short vowel (grin, grinning).

lessons.title: Getting to know a narrative
lessons.li: We are learning how a narrative begins and how the orientation sets up what we expect.
sc: I can share ideas using our talk protocols
I can name the main parts of a narrative
I can find the characters, setting and a hint of trouble
materials: Fantastic Mr Fox by Roald Dahl (cover hidden)
Orientation planner (one each, plus one enlarged)

slides.title: Warm-up: Stories we know
slides.prompt: Think of a story you love. Write quick answers.
answers: Answers will vary: a named character
slides.notes: This draws out what students already know about narrative from Stage 1. Keep a few answers to use when building the narrative anchor chart.

slides.title: Why we talk to learn

rows.label: Remember
rows.text: Saying an idea out loud helps us remember it.

rows.label: Stay alert
rows.text: Talking keeps our brain switched on.

rows.label: Connect
rows.text: We link ideas and fix mix-ups together.

rows.label: See more
rows.text: We hear how other people see things.

slides.notes: Ask students when talking with someone has helped them learn. Collect two or three examples before showing each row.

slides.title: Anchor chart: our talk protocols
points: Partner: we face each other and take turns
Partner: we listen to the end before we reply
Whole class: we raise a hand and wait
Whole class: we build on what others say
slides.notes: Co-construct these with the class and record them on the enlarged protocols poster. Leave the small group column for Lesson 2. We will come back to this chart all unit.

slides.title: Slow reveal
slides.intro: Cover hidden. I will read one sentence at a time.

steps.locator: Chapter 10, p 38: the first line of dialogue
questions: What type of text might this be?
Who could be talking, and to whom?

steps.locator: Chapter 10, p 38: the first sentence of the reply (leave out the speaker tag)
questions: Where might they be going?
Why would this place be so exciting?

steps.locator: Chapter 10, p 38: the next sentence of the reply
questions: Which words hint at a problem?
Why might they fail to get there?

steps.locator: Chapter 10, p 38: the last sentence of the reply
questions: How do these characters feel about each other?
Will that matter in the story? Why?

slides.notes: Read from your own copy, one sentence per slide. Keep the title and cover hidden until the end. Accept all predictions and ask students to give a reason.

slides.title: Reveal the cover
slides.prompt: Now look at the cover. What kind of text is this? Who is the main character, and what might he be like?
slides.notes: Invite connections to other Roald Dahl books students know. Tell them we will read this book together over the next five weeks.

slides.title: Anchor chart: a narrative
points: Purpose: to entertain the reader
Orientation: who, where and when
Complication: a problem to solve
Series of events: tries to fix the problem
Resolution: how it ends
slides.notes: Students first jot what they know about narratives on whiteboards. Build the chart from their ideas and add that characters, settings and events can be real or imagined. Keep this chart for Lesson 5.

slides.means: The start of a narrative. It tells us who is in the story, where and when it happens, and hints at a problem.
slides.example: Three farmers live in a valley, and a fox family lives in the wood above them.
slides.notes: Read Chapters 1 and 2 aloud now, without showing the illustrations, then show this slide.

slides.title: Meet the characters
rows: a hole under a big tree on the hill
slides.notes: Fill the blank cells with the class after reading Chapters 1 and 2. Bean keeps turkeys and apples. Mr Fox is a father who lives with Mrs Fox and four Small Foxes. Bunce's farm is also in the valley.

slides.title: What goes in an orientation
rows: Who is in the story? Who matters most?
Three farmers, Mr Fox and his family
Three farms in a valley, a wood on a hill
What makes us want to keep reading?
slides.notes: Model the first two rows from Chapters 1 and 2. These are the two boxes we fill in together before the activity. Ask the class for the hint of a problem and an engaging detail, then type them in.

slides.title: Is it part of an orientation?

yes.label: Where and when the story happens
A clue that trouble is coming

no.label: How the problem is finally solved

slides.notes: Thumbs up or down for each before revealing. The first non-example belongs in the resolution, not the orientation.

slides.title: Which one?
slides.question: Which detail is a hint of the problem?
options: Three farms are in the valley
Mr Fox has four Small Foxes
why: This is the setting. It tells us where, not what could go wrong.
Right. The farmers and the fox want opposite things, so trouble is coming.
This introduces characters. It does not tell us about a problem.
This is about the book itself, not the story inside it.
slides.notes: Students show 1 to 4 fingers. Anyone who chose A or C needs a quick reteach of the difference between setting, characters and problem.

slides.title: Activity: Orientation detectives
steps: Look at the two boxes we filled in together.
Fill in your own Orientation planner.
Use words and quick sketches.
Check each box with a partner.
slides.notes: Circulate and ask: How do you know? Where in the chapter did you find that?

slides.support: Draw the characters and setting in each box. Label one thing in each.
slides.core: Write key details from Chapters 1 and 2 in all five boxes.
slides.extend: Use your planner to write a 3 to 4 sentence summary of the orientation.

questions: What do you remember from today?
Why does a narrative need an orientation?
Which talk protocol helped you most today?
slides.connect: We learned that a narrative opens with an orientation that sets up who, where, when and a hint of trouble.
slides.notes: Students share with a partner first, then write one idea on a sticky note as they leave.

partner: We face our partner and take turns
We listen to the end before we reply
We ask a question when we are unsure
We share our partner's idea fairly
group: We give everyone a turn to speak
We keep our voices at group level
We build on each other's ideas
We agree before we share with the class
class: We raise a hand and wait our turn
We look at the person speaking
We say: I agree with ___ because ___
We respect opinions that differ from ours

prompts.details: What makes you want to read on?

lessons.teacherNotes: This lesson sets up the routines for the whole unit. Spend real time on the protocols because they are referred to in every lesson and assessed in Lesson 11. The slow reveal uses Chapter 10 because it shows characters, a setting and a problem without giving away the farmers. Keep the narrative anchor chart displayed for Lesson 5. Read Chapters 1 and 2 without the illustrations so students build their own pictures for Lesson 2.

exitTicket.q: Name two things an orientation tells the reader.
exitTicket.answer: Any two of: who the characters are, where the story is set, when it happens, a hint of the problem.

exitTicket.q: Write one detail from the orientation of Fantastic Mr Fox.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a character, the valley with three farms, the wood on the hill or the foxes' home under the tree.

lessons.title: Picturing characters
lessons.li: We are learning to use key words in a text to picture characters and make inferences about them.
sc: I can find key words that tell how a character looks and acts
I can make an inference from what a character says
I can draw and label a character using key words
materials: group copies of Chapter 1, pp 2 to 4 and Chapter 2, p 9

slides.title: Warm-up: Remember the orientation
slides.prompt: Write quick answers on your whiteboard.
items: What hint of trouble did we find?
answers: Boggis: chickens. Bunce: ducks and geese. Bean: turkeys and apples
In a hole under a big tree in the wood on the hill
The farmers want to stop Mr Fox taking their animals
slides.notes: Quick retrieval of Chapters 1 and 2 from Lesson 1.

slides.title: Anchor chart: small group protocols
points: We give everyone a turn to speak
We keep our voices at group level
We build on each other's ideas
We agree before we share with the class
slides.notes: Add these to the small group column of the protocols poster. Ask students which partner protocols also work in a group.

slides.means: How an author builds a character: how they look, act, think, feel and speak.
slides.example: We know a character is greedy when the author tells us she eats ten pies at every meal.
slides.notes: Explain that authors choose details so we see some characters as good and some as bad.

slides.title: Main and supporting characters
slides.prompt: Main: the story is about them. Supporting: they help, block or react. Drag each name.
slides.notes: Partners decide first, then students drag the cards on the board. Some may argue the farmers are main characters because they drive the plot. Accept this if they give a reason: the story is mostly about Mr Fox, and the farmers block him.

slides.title: How the author shows Boggis
slides.locator: Chapter 1, p 2: the paragraph beginning 'Boggis was a'
slides.task: Find the words that tell us how Boggis looks and what he eats.
questions: Which words show how big he is?
Which detail is exaggerated? Why?
How do you feel about Boggis? Which words do that?
slides.example: The giant ate [adj:forty] sausages [adv:every single morning].
slides.notes: Display your copy in the frame. Underline the key words with the class. Point out that the example sentence on the slide is ours and shows how exaggeration makes a character stand out.

slides.title: Bunce and Bean
slides.locator: Chapter 1, pp 3 to 4: the paragraphs beginning 'Bunce was a' and 'Bean was a'
slides.task: In your group, find key words about how your farmer looks and behaves.
questions: What does your farmer look like?
What does he eat or drink?
What kind of person is he? Which words tell you?
slides.notes: Half the groups take Bunce and half take Bean. Groups share their key words with the class.

slides.title: What we know about the farmers
rows: boiled chickens, three times a day
slides.notes: Groups report back and you type their key words into the table. Keep each cell to a few words. Bunce is short and pot-bellied, keeps ducks and geese, and has a nasty temper. Bean is thin, keeps turkeys and apples, drinks cider and is the cleverest.

slides.means: Working something out from clues in the text plus what you already know.
slides.example: Clue: he stamps his foot. I know: people stamp when they are cross. So: he is angry.
slides.notes: Model one inference out loud before the dialogue task.

slides.title: What the farmers say
slides.locator: Chapter 2, p 9: the farmers' conversation about Mr Fox
slides.task: Read the farmers' talk. Find words that show how Boggis thinks and feels.
questions: How does Boggis feel about Mr Fox? How do you know?
Why might he ask so many questions?
What new thing do we learn about the farmers?
slides.notes: Read the dialogue together, then groups look for more clues about their own farmer. Help students explain any unfamiliar insult words, then infer the feeling behind them.

slides.title: I do: picture Boggis

rows.label: Body
rows.text: Sketch his shape using the size words from page 2.

rows.label: Food
rows.text: Draw what he eats and label it with key words.

rows.label: Face
rows.text: Give him a face that matches how he talks in Chapter 2.

rows.label: Extra words
rows.text: Add my own labels, like [adj:greedy] and [adj:grumpy].

slides.notes: Think aloud as you draw and label on the board. Brainstorm more describing words that fit Boggis and add them as labels.

slides.title: Word bank: describing a character
points: Body: [adj:enormous], [adj:tiny], [adj:pot-bellied], [adj:skinny], [adj:hunched]
Face: [adj:scowling], [adj:pinched], [adj:greasy], [adj:sour]
Habits: [verb:gobbles], [verb:guzzles], [verb:grumbles], [verb:sneers]
Feelings: [adj:furious], [adj:frustrated], [adj:suspicious]
slides.notes: Add the class's own words in the blank row. Students can use this bank for their labels.

slides.title: Activity: Draw a farmer
steps: Choose Bunce or Bean.
Reread your group's key words.
Draw your farmer and add 4 labels from the text.
Add 2 describing words of your own.
slides.notes: Encourage words from Component A such as beastly and disgusting.

slides.support: Draw one farmer, then describe him to a partner using 3 key words.
slides.core: Draw Bunce or Bean with 4 labels from the text and 2 of your own words.
slides.extend: Write a short paragraph describing your farmer using your key words.

slides.title: Compare with the illustrator
slides.prompt: Look at the pictures on pages 2 to 4. How is your drawing the same? How is it different?
slides.notes: Show the illustrations now for the first time. Ask which key words the illustrator seems to have used.

questions: Which key word helped you most to picture your farmer?
How did your group use its protocols today?
slides.connect: We used key words to picture the farmers and made inferences from what they said.

data.locator: Chapter 1, pp 1 to 5: from 'Down in the valley' to the end of the chapter (about 245 words)

synopsis: Chapter 1 builds the world of the story: one valley, three farms, three unpleasant owners.
Each farmer gets a short portrait in the same pattern.
By the end, readers are firmly on the fox's side before he has even appeared.
structure: Setting: the valley and its farms
Farmer 1: name and job, farm, looks, what he eats
Farmer 2 and Farmer 3 follow the same pattern
A rhyme the local children chant about the farmers
language: Many declarative sentences that give facts
All three adjective types, before nouns and after the verb was
Comparisons that help us picture each farmer
Repeated sentence patterns and alliteration in the names

criteria: I drew my farmer using key words from the text
I added 4 labels from the text
I added 2 describing words of my own
data.drawPrompt: Draw your farmer here. Add 4 labels with key words from the text and 2 describing words of your own.

lessons.teacherNotes: Copy extracts from your own copy of the book under your school's statutory licence and include the required notice on each copy. The close reading planner is for you: use it to prepare the Chapter 1 discussion and the Component A fluency work. Do not show the illustrations until the end, so students build their own pictures from the words. Exaggeration is a big idea for this book, so name it whenever it comes up.

exitTicket.q: Write one key word that tells you what a farmer looks like. Name the farmer.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a word from Chapter 1 that matches the right farmer, such as fat (Boggis), short (Bunce) or thin (Bean).

exitTicket.q: Finish: I can infer that Boggis is ___ because ___.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a feeling such as angry or frustrated and a reason from his words or actions.

lessons.title: Creating a vivid character
lessons.li: We are learning to use declarative sentences and adjectives to create a vivid character.
sc: I can find declarative sentences in a character description
I can sort adjectives into quantifying, descriptive and classifying
I can write a character description with adjectives and commas

slides.title: Warm-up: Statement or not?
slides.prompt: Is it a declarative sentence? Write yes or no.
items: The shed was cold and dark.
slides.notes: This revises declarative sentences from Component A. Ask how students knew.

slides.title: Sentences that give facts
slides.locator: Chapter 1, pp 2 to 4: the three farmer paragraphs
slides.task: Find 3 declarative sentences. What does each one tell us?
questions: Why might the author use so many statements here?
How does each sentence end?
What is the same about how each paragraph starts?
slides.example: [noun:Farmer Pip] was a pumpkin-and-pear farmer.
slides.notes: Draw out that each paragraph starts with the farmer's name and job, then gives looks, food and personality. That is the pattern students will use.

slides.means: A word that describes, counts or groups a noun.
slides.example: Farmer Pip had [adj:muddy] boots and [adj:two] [adj:pumpkin] sheds.
slides.notes: Point out all three jobs an adjective can do in the example sentence.

slides.title: Three types of adjectives

rows.label: Quantifying
rows.text: How many or how much? [adj:three] hens, [adj:many] pears, [adj:twenty] geese

rows.label: Descriptive
rows.text: What is it like? [adj:enormous], [adj:grumpy], [adj:slimy], [adj:red]

rows.label: Classifying
rows.text: What kind? a [adj:pear] farmer, a [adj:tractor] shed, a [adj:duck] pond

slides.notes: Groups now sort the adjectives they found in the farmer paragraphs on the Adjective sort. Ask what the farmers would be like with only size and colour words.

slides.title: What type of adjective?
slides.question: In 'a pumpkin farmer', what type of adjective is pumpkin?
why: Pumpkin does not tell us how many.
Pumpkin does not tell us what the farmer is like.
Right. It tells us what kind of farmer she is.
It is a noun on its own, but here it describes the farmer, so it works as an adjective.
slides.notes: If many choose D, show that pumpkin answers the question what kind of farmer.

slides.title: Sort the adjectives
slides.prompt: Look at the adjective before each noun. Drag the card to its type.
slides.notes: Ask the three questions for each card: how many, what is it like, what kind? Students say the question that helped them as they drag.

slides.title: Commas between adjectives

rows.label: Rule
rows.text: When two or more describing adjectives sit before a noun, put a comma between them.

rows.label: Example
rows.text: She wore [adj:huge], [adj:muddy] boots.

rows.label: Test
rows.text: If you can say and between them, use a comma: huge and muddy boots.

slides.notes: Do a quick Think-Pair-Share: students add one more adjective to each category on their sort.

slides.title: I do: a fourth farmer
slides.intro: Watch how I build a new farmer, one fact at a time.

parts.label: Name and job
parts.text: Farmer Pip was a [adj:pumpkin-and-pear] farmer.

parts.label: Her farm
parts.text: She grew [adj:three thousand] pumpkins [adv:in a muddy field by Bluegum Creek].

parts.label: Looks
parts.text: She was [adj:tall], [adj:bony] and as stiff as a broom. Her boots were always caked in [adj:thick], [adj:brown] mud.

parts.label: Food
parts.text: She ate [adj:two] pumpkin pies and a bucket of pears [adv:at every meal].

parts.label: Personality
parts.text: All those pears made her [adj:grumpy]. She counted her pumpkins [adv:every night] because she trusted nobody.

slides.notes: Write this live, thinking aloud about each choice. Farmer Pip will appear in our model writing all unit, so introduce her properly. Point out the adverbial phrases of where and when too.

slides.title: Plan your farmer
rows: a muddy field by Bluegum Creek
pumpkin pies and a bucket of pears
slides.notes: Show how the model came from short plan notes, not full sentences. Take one class example for the right column, then students plan their own farmer the same way.

slides.title: Farmer Pip and Boggis
slides.prompt: How is our new farmer the same as Boggis? How is she different?
slides.notes: Add one more difference for Boggis with the class. Point out that a new character can borrow the pattern of a book character but still be someone new.

slides.title: Our success criteria
slides.stem: I can write a character description that includes:
points: the farmer's name and job first
declarative sentences that give facts
adjectives of all three types
commas between adjectives
capital letters for sentences and names
slides.notes: Build these with the class from the model. Leave a blank line for a criterion students suggest.

slides.title: Activity: Invent a fourth farmer
steps: With a partner, draw your farmer and label your ideas.
Plan: name and job, farm, looks, food, personality.
Write your description on the writing page.
Tick each success criterion as you go.
slides.notes: Students who finish early complete their level of the Adjectives and statements worksheet.

slides.support: Use the stems: Farmer ___ was a ___ farmer. She kept ___. She was ___.
slides.core: Write 5 to 7 declarative sentences that follow the farmer paragraph pattern.
slides.extend: Mix simple and compound sentences. Use and, but or so to join two facts.

slides.title: Peer feedback: Tell, Ask, Give
slides.notes: Revisit the partner protocols first. Partners use the success criteria and the TAG cards, then students revise one thing.

questions: Which adjective in your partner's work made the farmer easiest to picture?
What did you change after feedback?
slides.connect: We used declarative sentences and all three types of adjectives to create a vivid character.
slides.notes: Choose two or three students to read their farmer aloud and name the technique that worked.

teach.text: An adjective tells us more about a noun. In 'the muddy boot', muddy is the adjective.

items.q: Circle the adjective in each sentence.
Write a describing word for each noun.
Is it a statement? Write yes or no.
Fix the capital letters: farmer pip lived near bluegum creek.
items.answer: Farmer Pip lived near Bluegum Creek.

items.q: Write one statement about a farmer you invent. Use one adjective.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for a capital letter, an adjective and a full stop.

items.q: Expand the sentence with an adjective: The fox ran.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. The hungry fox ran.

teach.text: Quantifying adjectives tell how many. Descriptive adjectives tell what it is like. Classifying adjectives tell what kind. Put a comma between two describing adjectives.

items.q: Write Q, D or C for the adjective in capitals.
Add commas between the adjectives.

parts.q: It was a cold dark wet night.
parts.answer: It was a cold, dark, wet night.

items.q: Sort the words: twelve, slimy, apple, many, enormous, duck.
items.answer: Quantifying: twelve, many. Descriptive: slimy, enormous. Classifying: apple, duck.

items.q: Write 2 statements about Farmer Pip. Use 2 adjectives and a comma.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for statements with a comma between two adjectives, e.g. Farmer Pip had big, muddy boots.

items.q: Why do authors use lots of statements in a character description?
items.answer: Statements give the reader facts about the character, such as their job, looks and habits.

items.q: Expand the sentence with two adjectives and a comma: Pip has a dog.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. Pip has a loyal, scruffy dog.

teach.text: A compound adjective joins words with hyphens: a pumpkin-and-pear farmer. An adjective can also come after was: She was grumpy.

items.q: Make a compound adjective for a new farmer.
Write the adjective that comes after the verb.
Fix the sentence: farmer pip had a long dirty coat
items.answer: Farmer Pip had a long, dirty coat.

items.q: Rewrite with a stronger adjective: The farmer was very bad.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for a precise adjective such as cruel, nasty or wicked.

items.q: Join two facts with and, but or so: Pip grew pears. She never shared them.
items.answer: Pip grew pears, but she never shared them. (and is also acceptable)

items.q: Write a 3 sentence description of a fifth farmer using all 3 adjective types.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for a quantifying, a descriptive and a classifying adjective, and correct commas.

criteria: I start with the farmer's name and job
I use declarative sentences that give facts
I use quantifying, descriptive and classifying adjectives
I put commas between adjectives
I use capital letters for sentences and names

lessons.teacherNotes: Assessment task 1: collect the fourth farmer descriptions and observe the peer feedback (EN2-CWT-01: declarative sentences, adjectives, capital letters and commas between adjectives). Farmer Pip, her farm at Bluegum Creek and her Pumpkin Shed return in the model writing in Lessons 7, 8, 12, 13, 14 and the sequel in Week 5, so keep the model on display. Our model is written fresh in the same pattern as the mentor paragraphs, so students learn the structure without copying the book.

exitTicket.q: Add commas: The farmer had big muddy red boots.
exitTicket.answer: The farmer had big, muddy, red boots.

exitTicket.q: Write one declarative sentence about your farmer.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a complete statement that starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

lessons.title: Character traits and evidence
lessons.li: We are learning to identify a character's traits and back them up with evidence from the text.
sc: I can name a trait that fits a character
I can find evidence in the text for a trait
I can write about a trait using because or this shows
materials: Character trait bank (one per pair, plus one enlarged)
the Mr Fox trait wall slide (fox photo) on the board

slides.title: Warm-up: Adjectives and farmers
slides.prompt: Write quick answers on your whiteboard.
items: Write a classifying adjective for Farmer Pip.
Add commas: a tall bony grumpy farmer
Name one fact we know about Mr Fox's family.
Is greedy about looks or about the inside?
answers: Answers will vary: he lives with Mrs Fox and four Small Foxes under a tree
The inside: it is a trait
slides.notes: Retrieval of Lesson 3 adjectives and a lead-in to traits.

slides.title: Heroes and villains
slides.prompt: Who are the villains in this story so far? Who might be the hero? What in the text makes you think so?
slides.notes: Push students to point to a part of the text for each opinion.

slides.title: Foxes in other stories

rows.label: Fables
rows.text: In many fables and folk tales, the fox is a trickster.

rows.label: Picture books
rows.text: Think of the fox in Rosie's Walk or in Hattie and the Fox by Mem Fox.

rows.label: Our story
rows.text: Is Mr Fox the same as these foxes, or different?

slides.notes: Students turn and talk about what foxes are usually like in stories: sly, sneaky, clever. Then ask whether Mr Fox fits that pattern.

slides.title: Mr Fox at the start of Chapter 3
slides.locator: Chapter 3, pp 10 to 12: from the start of the chapter to the gunshots
slides.task: Compare Mr Fox here with Mr Fox in Chapter 2.
questions: What stays the same about Mr Fox?
What new thing do we learn about him?
Why might an author show a new side of a character?
slides.notes: Stop reading at the gunshots. The rest of Chapter 3 is read in Lesson 5. Students Think-Pair-Share the questions.

slides.means: A word that tells what a character is like on the inside, shown by what they do, say and think.
slides.example: Pip counts her pumpkins every night. She is suspicious.
slides.notes: Contrast traits with looks: tall and red are how a character looks, not what they are like inside.

slides.title: Is it a character trait?
slides.notes: Hungry is a close non-example: it is how a character feels right now, not what they are always like. Tall and red-haired are looks.

slides.title: Trait or not a trait?
slides.prompt: A trait is what a character is like on the inside. Add more words to each side.
headers: Not a trait (looks or a feeling for now)
slides.notes: Ask for words from the trait bank and from our talk. Feelings like hungry or sleepy change quickly, so they are not traits. Looks like tall are on the outside.

slides.title: Act out a trait
slides.intro: Cover the trait words. Guess the trait, then you try one from the trait bank.

rows.label: cautious
rows.text: Tiptoe to the door and peek slowly around it.

rows.label: cocky
rows.text: Strut about and brag loudly.

rows.label: loving
rows.text: Tuck a toy in gently and pat it.

rows.label: sly
rows.text: Grin and hide something behind your back.

slides.notes: Hide the left column. Act one out yourself, then invite students to choose traits from the trait bank to act for the class.

slides.title: I do: a trait with evidence
slides.intro: Watch me name a trait, give evidence, then explain.

parts.label: Trait
parts.text: Mr Fox is [adj:cautious].

parts.label: Evidence
parts.text: In Chapter 3, he creeps out of his hole slowly and sniffs the air before he moves.

parts.label: Explain
parts.text: This shows he knows the farmers could be waiting for him.

slides.notes: Name the pattern: trait, evidence, explain. Model a second trait orally using a moment from Chapter 2.

slides.title: Which is the best evidence?
slides.question: Trait: Mr Fox is loving. Which is the best evidence?
options: He brings food home each night
why: This is about looks, not what he is like inside.
Right. Bringing food home for his family shows he loves them.
This is the setting. It does not show a trait.
Being a fox is not evidence of any trait.
slides.notes: Students show fingers. Ask a student who chose B to explain the link between the action and the trait.

slides.title: Trait wall: Mr Fox

spokes.label: Cautious
spokes.text: sniffs the air before he leaves the hole

spokes.label: Loving
spokes.text: brings food home for his family

slides.notes: This is our trait wall. During the activity groups bring their sticky notes up. Type each new trait into a box and its evidence underneath. Rename the box with the trait.

slides.title: Activity: Trait detectives
steps: In your group, choose 3 traits from the trait bank.
Find evidence for each one in Chapter 2 or 3.
Write each trait and its evidence on a sticky note.
Stick your notes around the fox on our trait wall slide.
slides.notes: Build a verbal summary as a class. Draw out that Mr Fox is complex: clever and loving, but also cocky and sly.

slides.title: Write: a mini review of Mr Fox
steps: Pick 3 or 4 traits for Mr Fox.
For each one write: trait, evidence, explain.
Use because or this shows.

slides.support: Use the starters: Mr Fox is ___. One thing that shows this is ___.
slides.core: Write about 3 traits. Give evidence from the text for each one.
slides.extend: Add page numbers to your evidence and show how Mr Fox is more than one thing.

questions: Is Mr Fox a simple character or a complex one? Why?
How well did you use our partner, group and class protocols this week?
slides.connect: We named traits for Mr Fox and backed each one with evidence from the text.
slides.notes: For the protocol question, students hold 1 to 3 fingers against their chest to rate themselves, then a few explain why.

traits.means: shows love to family and friends
sticks by friends no matter what
not afraid to take a risk
keeps going and never gives up
quick to learn and work things out
finds a way with what they have
wants to find out about things
tricks others in a quiet way
a bit rude in a funny way
keeps thinking something bad will happen

teach.text: A trait tells what a character is like inside. Evidence is what they do or say that proves it.

items.q: Match each action to a trait: brave, greedy or kind.

parts.q: She ate all ten pies and wanted more.
He shared his lunch with a new boy.
She ran into the dark shed to save the cat.

items.q: Is it a trait (T) or how they look (L)?
Finish: Farmer Pip is suspicious because she ___.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for an action such as counting her pumpkins every night.

items.q: Finish: Mr Fox is ___. One thing that shows this is ___.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for a trait matched to an event, e.g. loving: he brings food home for his family.

items.q: Circle the trait word in each sentence.

parts.q: The cautious fox sniffed the air.

items.q: Draw a character and write 2 traits next to them.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for 2 inside traits, not looks.

teach.text: Trait, evidence, explain. Mr Fox is cautious. He creeps out slowly and sniffs. This shows he knows danger could be near.

items.q: Write a trait for each piece of evidence.

parts.q: He hides from the farmers and waits.
parts.answer: Answers will vary: cautious, patient or careful

parts.q: He uses kind, gentle names for his wife.
parts.answer: Answers will vary: loving or caring

parts.q: He tells his family the farmers are no match for him.
parts.answer: Answers will vary: cocky, confident or boastful

items.q: Write trait, evidence and explain for Mr Fox. Trait: clever.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for an event from Chapter 2 or 3 as evidence and an explanation of how it shows he is clever.

items.q: Write trait, evidence and explain for one of the farmers.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for a trait such as greedy or mean, backed by an event from Chapters 1 to 3.

items.q: Which word is a stronger trait than nice: caring, okay or good?
items.answer: caring

items.q: Fix the sentence so it gives evidence: Mr Fox is clever because he is clever.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for an action as evidence, e.g. Mr Fox is clever because he smells where the farmers are hiding.

items.q: Sort into trait or looks.

teach.text: Characters can show different traits at different times. Use but to show both sides: Mr Fox is loving, but he is also cocky.

items.q: Write a sentence that shows two sides of Mr Fox using but.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for two traits joined by but, e.g. Mr Fox is clever, but he can be careless.

items.q: How is Mr Fox like the fox in another story you know? How is he different?
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for a named story, one way they are alike (sly, clever) and one difference (a loving father).

items.q: Choose a trait for Mrs Fox and give evidence.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for a trait such as caring or sensible, with evidence such as warning Mr Fox to be careful.

items.q: Write a 4 sentence mini review of Mr Fox with 2 traits and page numbers.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for 2 traits, evidence with page numbers for each, and an explanation.

items.q: Which trait changes in Chapter 3 compared with Chapter 2? Explain.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. In Chapter 2 he seems cocky, but in Chapter 3 he is cautious when he leaves the hole.

items.q: Find a word in the trait bank that means the opposite of cautious. Use it in a sentence.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. daring, bold or fearless, used correctly in a sentence.

lessons.teacherNotes: Assessment task 2: observe the trait detective groups and collect the mini reviews (EN2-UARL-01: characters identified through familiar, individual or group characteristics). Mrs Fox's warnings to her husband are good evidence that he can be overconfident. Students may quote short phrases from the text as evidence in their own writing, which is fine for classroom use. Go back to the trait wall slide for the activity. At the end, move the sticky notes onto chart paper and keep them on display for Lesson 10.

exitTicket.q: Name one trait of Mr Fox and give evidence.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a trait such as clever, cautious, loving or cocky linked to an event from the text.

exitTicket.q: What is the difference between a trait and how a character looks?
exitTicket.answer: A trait is what a character is like inside, such as brave or greedy. Looks are outside features, such as tall or red.

lessons.title: Problems that drive a story
lessons.li: We are learning how a complication and a series of events drive a narrative forward.
sc: I can name the complication in a story
I can track events with Somebody, Wanted, But, So, Then
I can explain how failed attempts build tension
materials: Somebody, Wanted, But, So, Then chart (one per pair, plus a large class copy)

slides.title: Warm-up: The orientation
slides.prompt: Write quick answers on your whiteboard.
items: Where does the fox family live?
What does Mr Fox do each night?
Name one trait of Mr Fox.
answers: In a hole under a big tree in the wood on the hill
He goes down to the farms to take food for his family
Answers will vary: clever, cautious, loving or cocky
slides.notes: Retrieval of Week 1. Ask for evidence for the trait answer.

slides.title: What comes next?
slides.prompt: Look at our narrative anchor chart. Has the complication started yet? If so, what is it? If not, what might it be?
slides.notes: Point to the anchor chart from Lesson 1 as students talk.

slides.means: The problem in a narrative. It makes the characters act and keeps the reader wanting more.
slides.example: Farmer Pip wants to catch the pear thief, but the thief keeps getting away.
slides.notes: Explain that a complication is rarely fixed on the first try. Each failed try makes the reader more worried.

slides.title: Is it a complication?

yes.label: The farmers want to kill the fox
The wolf wants to eat the pigs

no.label: The farm has a red barn
The fox has a bushy tail

slides.notes: The last non-example is a resolution. The other two are setting and description.

slides.title: Somebody, Wanted, But, So, Then
points: Somebody: who is the main character?
Wanted: what is their goal?
But: what problem gets in the way?
So: what do they try?
Then: how does it end?
slides.notes: Explain that But and So can repeat many times in a story. Each new But is a new problem.

slides.title: I do: a story we all know
slides.intro: Watch me use the chart on The Three Little Pigs.

parts.label: Somebody
parts.text: The three little pigs

parts.label: Wanted
parts.text: to live safely in their own houses

parts.label: But
parts.text: a hungry wolf wanted to eat them.

parts.label: So
parts.text: they built houses of straw, sticks and bricks.

parts.label: But
parts.text: the wolf blew down the straw and stick houses.

parts.label: Then
parts.text: the brick house kept them all safe.

slides.notes: Point out the second But. Every time the characters try something and it fails, the tension goes up.

slides.title: Which is the complication?
slides.question: In Fantastic Mr Fox so far, what is the main problem?
options: The foxes live in a wood
Farmers want to stop Mr Fox
why: This is the setting.
Right. The farmers and the fox want opposite things.
This tells us about characters, not a problem.
This is a character detail that makes us dislike Boggis.
slides.notes: Then model the first rows for Fantastic Mr Fox: Somebody Mr Fox, Wanted to feed his family, But the farmers want to stop him stealing.

slides.title: Try, fail, try again
slides.prompt: Read Chapters 3 to 6. Fill in each So and But.

steps.label: But
steps.text: Mr Fox escapes. They only shoot his tail.

slides.notes: Model Chapter 3. After reading each chapter, type the next So and But with the class. Chapter 4: they dig with shovels, but the foxes dig deeper. Chapters 5 and 6: they bring huge digging machines, but the foxes dig faster and get away.

slides.title: Word bank: talking about plot
points: Time words: first, next, after that, then, finally
Problem words: but, however, unfortunately
Result words: so, because of this, as a result
Story words: attempt, fail, escape, plan
slides.notes: Students use these words when they share their charts orally.

slides.title: Activity: Track the tries
steps: Listen as I read each chapter.
After each chapter, add a So and a But to your chart.
Check with your partner that you agree.
Be ready to share one row with the class.
slides.notes: As pairs share, build the class chart. This class chart grows every week until the end of the unit.

slides.support: Tell a partner each So and But out loud. I will scribe one row with you.
slides.core: Write a So and a But for each chapter from 3 to 6 on your chart.
slides.extend: Add how each failure makes the reader feel, then predict the next So.

slides.title: Put the events in order
slides.prompt: Chapters 3 to 6. Drag the events into the right order.
items: The farmers wait outside the hole with guns.
Mr Fox escapes, but he loses his tail.
The foxes dig deeper to get away.
The farmers bring in giant digging machines.
The foxes race to dig faster and escape.
slides.notes: Students take turns to drag one strip and say a time word as they do: first, next, after that, finally.

slides.title: Show me: So or But?
slides.prompt: Write So or But.
questions: The farmers dug with shovels.
The foxes dug faster.
The farmers brought in machines.
The foxes dug deeper still.
slides.notes: Each So is an attempt and each But is a failure.

questions: Why don't the farmers win on their first try?
How do the failed attempts keep you reading?
slides.connect: We found the complication and tracked the try, fail, try again pattern that drives the story.

lessons.teacherNotes: Students cannot complete the Then row yet, because the ending comes in Chapter 17. That row is filled in Lesson 15. Keep the class chart on display and add to it in Lessons 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 15. Point out that the foxes and farmers have opposite goals: that clash is where tension comes from.

exitTicket.q: What is a complication?
exitTicket.answer: The main problem in a narrative that the characters try to solve.

exitTicket.q: Write one So and one But from Chapters 4 to 6.
exitTicket.answer: So the farmers dug with shovels, but the foxes dug faster. (or: So they used machines, but the foxes dug deeper.)

reallife.title: A tunnel under the hill

items.caption: An animal tunnel under tree roots. Imagine creeping up one like this at night.

reallife.question: What might you hear, smell and see at the mouth of a tunnel at night?

lessons.li: We are learning how authors use action verbs and adverbial phrases to change the pace and build tension.
sc: I can find small steps that slow the action down
I can name action verbs and explain their effect
I can sort adverbial phrases into when, where, how and why
materials: Action verbs and adverbial phrases worksheet

slides.title: Warm-up: The farmers' tries
slides.prompt: Write quick answers on your whiteboard.
items: What was the farmers' first try?
answers: Waiting with guns outside the hole
Mr Fox was too quick, then the foxes dug faster and deeper
slides.notes: Retrieval of Lesson 5.

slides.title: Chapters 7 and 8: a new problem

rows.label: The tries stop
rows.text: The farmers stop digging, but they do not give up. They camp around the hole and wait.

rows.label: New problem
rows.text: The foxes are trapped underground and starting to starve.

rows.label: Our chart
rows.text: Add a new But to the class Somebody, Wanted, But, So, Then chart.

slides.notes: Read Chapters 7 and 8 first. Then add the new problem to the class chart.

slides.means: The worried, edge-of-your-seat feeling a reader gets when something bad might happen.
slides.example: The stairs creaked. Someone was coming.
slides.notes: Ask students where in a book or film they have felt this. Tension makes us keep reading.

slides.title: Slow steps in Chapter 3
slides.locator: Chapter 3, pp 10 to 12: from 'Mr Fox crept up' up to 'Just then, his sharp'
slides.task: As I read, act out each small step Mr Fox takes. Count the steps.
questions: How many small steps did Mr Fox take?
Why are the sentences so short here?
What does each full stop make the reader do?
How do the verbs help you hear the scene?
slides.example: Biscuit [verb:lifted] her head. She [verb:sniffed]. She [verb:waited].
slides.notes: Students stand and act as Mr Fox while you read. List the steps on the board: each one starts with an action verb. Our example sentence shows the same trick with new characters.

slides.title: Action verbs
slides.prompt: Strong verbs help us see the action. Swap it: Mr Fox went out. Mr Fox crept out.
slides.notes: Act out a pair of verbs from each row. Ask which column fits a tense, careful moment and which fits a sudden one.

slides.title: Adverbial phrases
slides.intro: An adverbial phrase adds detail to a verb.

rows.label: When
rows.text: The fox [verb:crept] out [adv:at midnight].

rows.label: Where
rows.text: The fox [verb:crept] [adv:along the creek bank].

rows.label: How
rows.text: The fox [verb:crept] [adv:without a sound].

rows.label: Why
rows.text: The fox [verb:crept] out [adv:to find food].

slides.notes: Pairs find adverbial phrases in the first part of the passage and label each one when, where, how or why. Share and justify.

slides.title: Sort the adverbial phrases
slides.prompt: Which question does each phrase answer? Drag it to when, where, how or why.
slides.notes: Say each phrase in a sentence first: The fox crept out at midnight. Then ask: does it tell when, where, how or why?

slides.title: Show me: when, where, how or why?
slides.prompt: Write the question each phrase answers.
questions: The fox waited behind the shed.
The fox waited until dark.
The fox waited with great patience.
The fox waited to grab a hen.
slides.notes: Reread the passage for students to act again, this time slower and with more detail.

slides.title: The pace speeds up
slides.locator: Chapter 3, pp 12 to 13: from 'Just then, his sharp' to the end of the chapter
slides.task: Find the words that make the action go fast.
questions: Which time words tell us it happens suddenly?
Which verbs are fast?
Why are some words in italics with exclamation marks?
How is this part different from the first part?
slides.example: [adv:All at once], the cans [verb:crashed] [adv:to the floor]. Clang!
slides.notes: Draw out time phrases, fast verbs, Mr Fox's thoughts and sound words. Read it a final time for students to act, showing the sudden change.

slides.title: Word bank: changing the pace
points: Slow down: then, slowly, inch by inch, one paw at a time
Speed up: suddenly, all at once, in a flash, without warning
Sound words: rustle, creak, clang, crash, bang
Short sentences: Nothing. He froze. Silence.
slides.notes: Students will use this bank in Lessons 7 and 8.

slides.title: How else could they catch him?
slides.prompt: Brainstorm new ways the farmers could try to catch Mr Fox. Then think: how might each one fail?
slides.notes: Groups record plans and fails side by side. These ideas are used in Lesson 7.

slides.title: Activity: Plans and fails
steps: In your group, list 4 ways to catch Mr Fox.
Next to each one, write how it could fail.
Then do your level of the Action verbs and adverbial phrases sheet.

slides.support: List 2 catch plans and act out how each one fails. Circle the action verbs on your sheet.
slides.core: List 4 plans with fails, then complete the verbs and adverbial phrases sheet.
slides.extend: Write each plan and its fail as a compound sentence using but.

questions: How did the author slow down and then speed up the action?
Which plan from your group would make the best story? Why?
slides.connect: We found how action verbs, small steps and adverbial phrases control the pace and build tension.

data.locator: Chapter 3, pp 10 to 13: from 'Mr Fox crept up' to the end of the chapter (about 290 words)

synopsis: The farmers' first attempt to get rid of Mr Fox.
They wait outside his hole with guns, placed so he cannot smell them.
Mr Fox comes out slowly, senses danger and dives back as they fire.
structure: Mr Fox leaves the den in slow, careful steps
He senses something is wrong and stops
He spots the danger and the action speeds up
language: Adverbial phrases of place, time and manner picture each move
Sound words help us hear the scene
Slow verbs first, then fast verbs, so the pace changes
Mr Fox's thoughts bring us close to him

teach.text: An action verb is a doing word: run, creep, jump. An adverbial phrase tells when, where, how or why.

items.q: Circle the action verb.
Write a stronger verb for went.

parts.q: The fox went quietly to the shed.
parts.answer: Answers will vary: crept, tiptoed or sneaked

parts.q: The dog went fast across the yard.
parts.answer: Answers will vary: raced, dashed or bolted

items.q: Does the phrase tell when or where?
Expand the sentence with a where phrase: The fox hid.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for a place phrase, e.g. The fox hid behind the hay bales.

items.q: Slow or fast verb?
Draw the fox creeping and write one sentence with an action verb.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for an action verb such as crept.

teach.text: Adverbial phrases answer when, where, how or why. At dawn (when) the fox crept along the fence (where).

items.q: Write when, where, how or why.
Sort the verbs into slow or fast: dashed, inched, crept, leapt, tiptoed, bolted.
items.answer: Slow: inched, crept, tiptoed. Fast: dashed, leapt, bolted.

items.q: Expand with a how phrase: Mr Fox sniffed the air.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for a manner phrase, e.g. Mr Fox sniffed the air with his nose held high.

items.q: Fix the weak verb: The farmer got out of bed and went to the shed.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. The farmer leapt out of bed and stomped to the shed.

items.q: Underline the adverbial phrases: After dinner, Pip walked to the creek to fetch water.
items.answer: After dinner (when), to the creek (where), to fetch water (why)

items.q: Write 3 short sentences that show a character creeping towards danger, one small step each.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for 3 short sentences with action verbs, e.g. She opened the gate. She stopped. She listened.

teach.text: Short sentences slow the reader down and build tension. Fast verbs and time phrases like all at once speed it up.

items.q: Label the adverbial phrases: At dawn, the fox crept along the fence to find food.
items.answer: At dawn (when), along the fence (where), to find food (why)

items.q: Rewrite to slow it down using 3 short sentences: The fox walked to the shed and opened the door.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. The fox crept to the shed. He stopped. Slowly, he nudged the door open.

items.q: Rewrite to speed it up with a fast verb and a time phrase: The dog came out.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. All at once, the dog shot out of its kennel.

items.q: Write a plan to catch Mr Fox and how it fails, as one compound sentence with but.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. The farmers rigged a loud alarm, but the foxes chewed through the wire.

items.q: Write a sentence with an adverbial phrase of why.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for a reason phrase, e.g. Badger dug all night to reach the cellar.

items.q: Explain why an author might use a sound word like Bang! here.
items.answer: Answers will vary: it helps the reader hear the moment and makes the action feel sudden and fast.

lessons.teacherNotes: Copy extracts from your own copy of the book under your school's statutory licence and include the required notice on each copy. The Chapter 3 passage is also the Component A fluency passage this week, so students will know it well. Spend most of the time on the two halves of the scene: slow, careful steps first, then a sudden burst of speed. The plans and fails lists are needed for Lesson 7, so collect them.

exitTicket.q: Write 2 slow action verbs and 2 fast action verbs.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: slow such as crept, inched, tiptoed; fast such as leapt, dashed, raced.

exitTicket.q: Write the adverbial phrase and its question: Mr Fox hid behind the tree.
exitTicket.answer: behind the tree (where)
