lessons.li: We are learning to write an event that builds tension using action verbs and adverbial phrases.
sc: I can break an event into small steps
I can use action verbs and adverbial phrases in my sentences
I can use simple and compound sentences with punctuation
materials: plans and fails lists from Lesson 6

slides.title: Warm-up: Find the phrase
slides.prompt: Write the adverbial phrase and the question it answers.
items: At sunset, the fox woke up.
Biscuit growled in a low voice.
Badger dug to reach the cellar.

slides.title: Remember Farmer Pip?

rows.label: The problem
rows.text: Someone keeps stealing pears from Pip's Pumpkin Shed. She is sure it is Mr Fox.

rows.label: Her plan
rows.text: Pip ties tin cans on a string across the shed door. If the fox trips it, the cans will clang.

rows.label: Your turn
rows.text: Choose one plan from your group's list in Lesson 6.

slides.notes: Remind students of Farmer Pip from Lesson 3. Today we write how she sets up her plan. Next lesson, Mr Fox arrives.

slides.title: I do: small steps
slides.intro: First I list the steps. Each one has an action verb.

parts.text: Pip [verb:dragged] a sack of tin cans [adv:out of the Pumpkin Shed].
She [verb:threaded] the cans [adv:onto a long string].
She [verb:stretched] the string [adv:across the doorway].
She [verb:sprinkled] flour [adv:over the floor] to show footprints.
Pip and Biscuit [verb:crouched] [adv:behind the hay bales] and [verb:waited].

slides.notes: Write the steps as a list first. Point out the verb and the adverbial phrase in each.

slides.title: Act it out
slides.prompt: With a partner, act out the 5 steps. Does the order make sense? What would you add or change?
slides.notes: Acting out checks that the storyline makes sense to an audience.

slides.title: Put Pip's steps in order
slides.prompt: Drag Pip's small steps into an order that makes sense.
items: Pip drags a sack of tin cans out of the shed.
She threads the cans onto a long string.
She stretches the string across the doorway.
She sprinkles flour over the floor.
Pip and Biscuit crouch behind the hay and wait.
slides.notes: After acting it out, students order the strips. Ask: could any steps swap? Which step must come last?

slides.title: Is it a small step?

yes.label: She threaded the cans onto a string.
She tied the string to a nail.

no.label: She set a trap and caught him.

slides.notes: The non-examples skip the action or tell instead of show. A small step is one clear action we can picture.

slides.title: Our success criteria
slides.stem: I can write a narrative event that builds tension and includes:
points: small steps in the right order
action verbs that set the pace
adverbial phrases for when, where, how or why
simple and compound sentences
capital letters and full stops

slides.title: I do: steps into sentences
slides.intro: Watch how I turn my list into a paragraph.

parts.label: Opening
parts.text: [adv:As the sun sank behind the hill], Farmer Pip got to work.

parts.label: Steps 1 and 2
parts.text: She [verb:dragged] a sack of rusty tin cans out of the Pumpkin Shed. [adv:Carefully], she [verb:threaded] them onto a long, thin string.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.text: She [verb:stretched] the string [adv:across the doorway] and tied it tight [adv:to a bent nail].

parts.label: Step 4
parts.text: Next, she [verb:sprinkled] flour [adv:over the floor], so every footprint would show.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.text: Then Pip [verb:blew out] her lantern, [verb:crouched] [adv:behind the hay bales] with Biscuit, and [verb:waited].

slides.notes: Think aloud: where can I add when, where or how? Where can I join two steps with and or so? Tick the success criteria together.

slides.title: Which sentence builds the most tension?
slides.question: Which sentence builds the most tension?
options: Pip put cans on a string.
Pip was a farmer with a dog.
why: This tells us, but gives no small steps or detail.
Better, but put is a weak verb and nothing slows the moment down.
Right. A slow how word and a precise verb help us picture each step.
This is a character fact, not part of the event.

slides.title: Word bank: setting up a plan
points: Verbs: [verb:dragged], [verb:hauled], [verb:hammered], [verb:tied], [verb:hid], [verb:crouched]
Time connectives: first, next, then, after that, finally
Where: [adv:behind the hay], [adv:across the doorway], [adv:under the gate]
How: [adv:carefully], [adv:with a sly grin], [adv:without a sound]

slides.title: Plan your set-up
slides.notes: Show that each small step needs one strong verb and often one phrase. Fill steps 3 and 4 with the class from the model, then students plan their own plan the same way.

slides.title: Activity: Plan and write the set-up
steps: Choose your plan to catch Mr Fox.
List 4 to 6 small steps, each with an action verb.
Act it out with a partner to rehearse.
Write your paragraph on the writing page.

slides.support: Act out the event with me. Use our list of action verbs to write 3 to 4 sentences.
slides.core: Turn your 4 to 6 steps into a paragraph with action verbs and adverbial phrases.
slides.extend: Use a thesaurus to choose more precise action verbs. Swap at least 3.

slides.title: Peer feedback: Tell, Ask, Give
slides.notes: Partners use the success criteria and the TAG cards. Students then revise their paragraph using the feedback.

questions: Which action verb in your writing are you proudest of?
Where did you use a compound sentence?
slides.connect: We broke an event into small steps and used action verbs and adverbial phrases to build tension. Next lesson, Mr Fox arrives.

criteria: small steps in the right order
action verbs that set the pace
adverbial phrases for when, where, how or why
simple and compound sentences
capital letters and full stops

lessons.teacherNotes: The model plan is our own: Farmer Pip's tin can alarm in her Pumpkin Shed. Students choose their own plan from their Lesson 6 list, and it does not have to involve Farmer Pip. Rehearsing by acting out is important for students who find writing hard. Share two or three paragraphs at the end that show clear small steps.

exitTicket.q: Write one small step with an action verb and an adverbial phrase.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for e.g. Pip crept behind the hay bales.

exitTicket.q: Why do authors break an event into small steps?
exitTicket.answer: To slow the action down so the reader feels the tension.

lessons.title: Writing tension: the escape
lessons.li: We are learning to finish an event by slowing the action down, then speeding it up.
sc: I can write slow small steps that build tension
I can speed up the action with short sentences and fast verbs
I can use exclamations and sound words for effect

slides.title: Warm-up: Slow or fast?
slides.prompt: Write slow or fast.

slides.title: Remember the shooting scene
slides.locator: Chapter 3, pp 10 to 13: the whole scene
slides.task: Reread and point to where the pace changes.
questions: Where does it change from slow to fast?
What word or phrase signals the change?
How does the last line make you feel?
slides.notes: Also reread your Lesson 7 model so students remember Farmer Pip's plan.

slides.title: I do: Mr Fox's slow steps
slides.intro: First I list his steps as he walks into the plan.

parts.text: Mr Fox [verb:poked] his nose [adv:out of the tunnel].
He [verb:sniffed] the cold air.
He [verb:crept] [adv:across the yard], one paw at a time.
He [verb:smelt] ripe pears [adv:through the gap in the door].
He [verb:spotted] a thin line of string [adv:near the ground].

slides.notes: Students act out the steps, with one student as Mr Fox and one as Farmer Pip hiding.

slides.title: I do: the slow paragraph
slides.intro: Watch how I turn the steps into a slow, tense paragraph.

parts.label: Scene
parts.text: The night was still and silent.

parts.label: Step 1 and 2
parts.text: Mr Fox [verb:poked] his nose [adv:out of the tunnel] and [verb:sniffed] the cold air. Nothing.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.text: He [verb:crept] [adv:across the yard], one paw at a time. [adv:At the shed door] he stopped.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.text: The smell of ripe pears drifted through the gap, so he [verb:inched] forward. His whiskers [verb:twitched].

parts.label: Danger
parts.text: A thin line of string [verb:glinted] [adv:in the moonlight], just above the ground.

slides.notes: Point out the one word sentence: Nothing. Short sentences make the reader hold their breath.

slides.title: Slow it down, speed it up
rows: Time words: then, slowly, inch by inch
Time words: all at once, in a flash, without warning
Fast verbs: leapt, spun, bolted, crashed
Short bursts: Too late! Run! He froze.
Quiet sounds: a rustle, a creak
slides.notes: Read across each row. The left side is what we used in the slow paragraph. The right side is what we will use for the fast ending.

slides.title: I do: the fast ending
slides.intro: Now the action explodes. Listen to how quick it feels.

parts.label: Too late
parts.text: Too late! His back paw [verb:caught] the string.

parts.label: Sound
parts.text: Clang! Clatter! Bang! The cans [verb:crashed] [adv:across the floor].

parts.label: Reaction
parts.text: 'Fox!' roared Farmer Pip. Biscuit [verb:leapt] [adv:over the hay bales].

parts.label: Escape
parts.text: [adv:In a flash], Mr Fox [verb:spun] around and [verb:bolted] [adv:into the dark].

parts.label: Safe
parts.text: He did not stop running until he was safe in his tunnel.

slides.notes: Read the slow and fast paragraphs together so students feel the change in pace.

slides.title: Slow, then fast
slides.prompt: Drag the events of the escape into order. Where does it speed up?
items: Mr Fox pokes his nose out of the tunnel.
He creeps across the yard, one paw at a time.
He smells ripe pears through the gap.
He spots a thin line of string.
Too late! His back paw catches the string.
Clang! The cans crash and Biscuit leaps.
In a flash, he bolts into the dark.
slides.notes: Once the strips are in order, ask students to point to where the pace changes. The answer is strip 5, Too late.

slides.title: Does it speed up the action?

yes.label: In a flash, he was gone.

no.label: The night was long and quiet.
He thought about it for a while.

slides.notes: The non-examples use slow verbs or long, calm sentences.

slides.title: Show me: speed it up
slides.prompt: Rewrite each one to make it faster.
questions: The dog started to run after him.
The cans fell down and made a noise.
The fox turned around and went home.
Pip got up from where she was hiding.
answers: Answers will vary: e.g. Biscuit shot after him!
Answers will vary: e.g. Crash! The cans clattered down.
Answers will vary: e.g. In a flash, the fox spun and bolted home.
Answers will vary: e.g. Pip leapt up from the hay!

slides.title: Our success criteria
slides.stem: I can write a narrative event that builds tension and includes:
points: slow small steps, then a fast ending
action verbs that set the pace
adverbial phrases for when, where, how or why
an exclamation or sound word at the exciting moment
capital letters, full stops and exclamation marks
slides.notes: These extend the Lesson 7 criteria.

slides.title: Activity: Finish your event
steps: Act out Mr Fox's response to your plan.
Write the slow steps as he gets closer.
Switch to fast sentences when he spots the danger.
Check the success criteria.

slides.support: Write 3 slow sentences and 2 fast ones. Use the verb lists on the slides.
slides.core: Write a slow paragraph, then a fast one, using our success criteria.
slides.extend: Add Mr Fox's thoughts and a sound word, then end with a twist.

slides.title: Peer feedback: Tell, Ask, Give
slides.notes: Partners check for the change of pace. Students revise one sentence to make it slower or faster.

questions: Where does your pace change? Show your partner.
What did you revise after feedback?
slides.connect: We slowed the action down with small steps, then sped it up with short sentences, fast verbs and sound words.

criteria: slow small steps, then a fast ending
action verbs that set the pace
adverbial phrases for when, where, how or why
an exclamation or sound word at the exciting moment
capital letters, full stops and exclamation marks

lessons.teacherNotes: Students continue their own Lesson 7 plan. The model continues Farmer Pip's tin can alarm: Mr Fox walks in slowly, spots the string too late, and escapes in a burst of fast sentences. Keep both model paragraphs on display. Many students overuse exclamation marks at this stage, so remind them to save them for the most exciting moment.

exitTicket.q: Write a short sentence that speeds up the action.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a short sentence with a fast verb or sound word, e.g. Crash! He bolted.

exitTicket.q: Name one way to slow the action down.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: small steps, short sentences with full stops, slow verbs like crept or inched.

lessons.title: Visualising settings

reallife.title: A valley and a wood

items.caption: Farms down in a valley, with a wood on the hill above. Our story uses a setting like this.

reallife.question: Where would you put the three farms and the foxes' hole?

lessons.li: We are learning to use key words in a text to picture settings and show them on a story map.
sc: I can follow our group protocol when we retell
I can find key words that describe a setting
I can draw and label a story map with my group
materials: Story map page, printed at A3 (one per group)
class Somebody, Wanted, But, So, Then chart

slides.title: Warm-up: Pace and tension
slides.prompt: Write quick answers on your whiteboard.
items: Write a time phrase that speeds things up.
Why do authors use small steps?
answers: Answers will vary: crept, inched, tiptoed
Answers will vary: leapt, bolted, dashed
Answers will vary: all at once, in a flash, suddenly
To slow the action down and build tension

slides.title: Our group focus
points: We acknowledge each other's ideas
We say: I agree with ___ because ___
We build on what others say
We give everyone a turn to retell
slides.notes: Groups choose one protocol as their focus today and describe what success will look and sound like. You will check in on it during the lesson.

slides.title: Retell chapter by chapter

rows.label: How
rows.text: Use each chapter title or first page as a memory cue.

rows.label: Who
rows.text: Take turns: one chapter each around the group.

rows.label: Words
rows.text: Use our new words: beastly, cautious, tension, complication.

slides.notes: Groups rehearse retelling Chapters 1 to 8. Pause after five minutes to reflect on their protocol focus.

slides.title: Retell: Chapters 1 to 9
slides.prompt: Drag the big events into order, then retell around your group.
items: We meet three farmers and a fox family.
The farmers shoot off Mr Fox's tail.
The farmers camp around the hole and wait.
Mr Fox thinks of a new plan.
slides.notes: Use this as the memory cue before the group retell. Each group member takes one strip and retells that part.

slides.title: Chapter 9: a new plan

rows.label: Mood
rows.text: The foxes are desperate and very hungry.

rows.label: Clue
rows.text: Mr Fox is silent for a long time while he thinks hard.

rows.label: Chart
rows.text: Add a new So to our class chart.

slides.notes: Read Chapter 9. Ask how the author shows desperation through actions and silence rather than telling us.

slides.means: Where and when a story happens. It can be real or imagined.
slides.example: Pip's farm sits in a damp valley beside Bluegum Creek, late in autumn.
slides.notes: Students Think-Pair-Share what they know about the setting so far. For example, the story is set in a valley with three farms.

slides.title: Is it about the setting?

yes.label: a wood on a hill above the valley
late at night, under the moon
a muddy hole under a tree

slides.notes: Setting is where and when. The non-examples are about characters' traits and feelings.

slides.title: Setting clues in Chapters 1 to 9
slides.locator: Chapter 1, p 1; Chapter 2, p 7; Chapter 2, p 8; Chapter 6, p 28; Chapter 7, p 31
slides.task: Scan these pages for key words that help you picture each place.
questions: Where are the farms?
Where is the foxes' home?
How does the hill change after the digging?
Where do the farmers camp?
slides.example: Bluegum Creek Farm sat [adv:at the bottom of a damp, green valley].
slides.notes: Model scanning one page aloud, then pairs scan the rest. Record key words on the board under each place.

slides.title: Our settings so far
rows: The farms are close together, below the wood.
slides.notes: Groups scan the pages and give one or two key words per place. Type them in, then talk about what each setting tells us about the characters or the danger.

slides.title: Word bank: setting words
points: Places: valley, hill, wood, burrow, tunnel, crater, orchard, shed
Where phrases: [adv:down in the valley], [adv:on top of the hill], [adv:deep underground]
Adjectives: [adj:muddy], [adj:gloomy], [adj:steep], [adj:enormous], [adj:silent]
When phrases: [adv:at night], [adv:at dawn], [adv:three days later]

slides.title: I do: start a story map

rows.label: Valley
rows.text: Draw three farms down low. Label each farm with its owner and animals.

rows.label: Hill
rows.text: Draw the wood on the hill and the big tree. Label with key words.

rows.label: The hole
rows.text: Show the crater, the tents and the hole. Number events where they happen.

slides.notes: Model on an A3 sheet in front of the class, thinking aloud about which key words to use as labels.

slides.title: Activity: Group story map
steps: Use your A3 story map page.
Draw the settings from Chapters 1 to 9.
Label each place with key words from the text.
Number the events where they happened.
slides.notes: Check in on each group's protocol focus and give feedback.

slides.support: Use the setting cards to label your map, and glue them in place.
slides.core: Draw and label all settings from Chapters 1 to 9 with key words from the text.
slides.extend: Add the underground tunnels below the hill, with labels from the text.

slides.title: Predict
slides.prompt: Look at your map. Where do you think the next events will happen? Why?
slides.notes: Then read Chapters 10 and 11 to confirm predictions. Groups add to their maps and you add to the class chart.

questions: Which key word helped your group picture a setting best?
How well did your group use its protocol focus?
slides.connect: We used key words from the text to picture the settings and show them on a story map.

printables.title: Setting cards
printables.instructions: Cut out. Read each card, then glue it on the right place on your story map.

cards.text: three farms down in the valley
a wood on the hill above
a huge tree with a hole beneath it
a giant crater where the hill was

lessons.teacherNotes: The setting cards are our own wording, so Get started groups can label a map without needing to copy from the book. Story maps are used again in Lesson 10, so keep them safe. If you have devices, groups could build the map digitally with drawing tools. Chapters 10 and 11 are read at the end of this lesson.

exitTicket.q: Name two settings from the story so far.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. the valley with three farms, the wood on the hill, the foxes' hole under the tree.

exitTicket.q: What is a setting?
exitTicket.answer: Where and when a story happens.

lessons.title: Vivid descriptions
lessons.li: We are learning how adjectives and adverbial phrases build vivid descriptions of characters and settings.
sc: I can give a trait for a character with evidence
I can find adjectives and phrases that exaggerate
I can show what too little and too much description looks like
materials: copies of the Chapter 10 and Chapter 13 passages

slides.title: Warm-up: Settings so far
slides.prompt: Write quick answers on your whiteboard.
items: Where did Mr Fox tunnel to in Chapter 10?
Name a descriptive adjective for a shed.
answers: Answers will vary: three, many, hundreds
Answers will vary: huge, dusty, creaky
Answers will vary: under the floor, along the wall

slides.title: Traits for the family
slides.prompt: Choose a trait from the trait bank for Mrs Fox or the Small Foxes. What did they do that shows it?
slides.notes: Students justify with an action from the text.

slides.title: New characters, bigger problem

rows.label: Badger
rows.text: Badger and his family are starving underground too.

rows.label: Bigger problem
rows.text: Now many animal families need food, not just the foxes.

rows.label: Hero
rows.text: They turn to Mr Fox for help, and he leads them.

slides.notes: Read Chapters 12 and 13 first. Ask why the author added new characters here. Discuss how Mr Fox directs the others in his long speech, which makes him the hero. Add to the class chart.

slides.title: Boggis's Chicken House
slides.locator: Chapter 10, pp 39 to 40: from 'Carefully, Mr Fox began' for about 240 words
slides.task: Find adjectives and phrases that describe the setting.
questions: Which words help you picture the shed?
Which phrase shows how excited the Small Foxes are?
Which adverbial phrases tell where?
How does the setting make you feel?
slides.example: The hens [verb:flapped] [adv:in every direction]!
slides.notes: Students turn and talk to find adjectives first, then adverbial phrases.

slides.title: Bunce's Giant Storehouse
slides.locator: Chapter 13, pp 50 to 51: from 'He reached high and' for about 240 words
slides.task: Find words that exaggerate size, number and quality.
questions: Which words make the storehouse seem huge?
Which words tell how many things there are?
Which words tell us the food is the best?
What if the author had used big or many instead?
slides.example: Pip's shed held [adj:hundreds and hundreds of] [adj:fat], [adj:orange] pumpkins!
slides.notes: Compare an exaggerating word with a plain one each time. Big is weaker than mighty; many is weaker than a huge number.

slides.title: Compare the storehouses
slides.notes: Our model row is filled. Take ideas for the two book settings from the passages we just read, using only a few key words per cell.

slides.title: Too little, too much, just right

rows.label: Too little
rows.text: Pip's shed had food.

rows.label: Too much
rows.text: Pip's huge, giant, enormous, massive shed was full of yummy, tasty, delicious, lovely food.

rows.label: Just right
rows.text: Pip's [adj:enormous] Pumpkin Shed was piled [adv:to the rafters] with [adj:ripe], [adj:orange] pumpkins.

slides.notes: Read each one aloud. Ask: which one helps you picture the shed? Which one is tiring to read? Why?

slides.title: Which is just right?
slides.question: Which sentence describes the setting best?
why: Too little: we cannot picture anything.
Too much: three words that mean the same thing, and it is not a full sentence.
Right. One precise adjective and a clear picture.
Not a sentence, and no description.

slides.title: Too little, too much, just right
slides.prompt: Drag each card. Is there too little, too much or just the right description?
cards: a huge, giant, big, large shed
lots and lots and lots of ducks

Too much: a huge, giant, big, large shed
lots and lots and lots of ducks

slides.notes: For each too much card, ask which one word they would keep. For each too little card, ask what one detail would help us picture it.

slides.title: Word bank: exaggeration
points: Size: [adj:mighty], [adj:gigantic], [adj:towering], [adj:bottomless]
Number: [adj:hundreds of], [adj:countless], [adj:a mountain of]
Quality: [adj:finest], [adj:juiciest], [adj:plumpest]
How: [adv:in every direction], [adv:with pure joy], [adv:at top speed]

slides.title: Activity: Too little, too much
steps: Pick a sentence from one of the passages.
Rewrite it with too little description.
Rewrite it with too much description.
Talk: why is the author's version better?
slides.notes: Students work on whiteboards or in their books.

slides.title: Activity: Inside the storehouses
steps: Add the inside of the Chicken House and the Storehouse to your story map.
Label them with adjectives and adverbial phrases.
Use clues from the chapter, not just what is said outright.
slides.notes: Show students how small clues let us infer more, such as a creaking floor suggesting old boards.

slides.support: Use the just right example to help you label your map with 4 adjectives.
slides.core: Write a too little and a too much version, then label your map with adjectives and phrases.
slides.extend: Write your own just right sentence about one setting and explain your word choices.

slides.title: Compare with the illustrations
slides.prompt: Look at the pictures on pages 39, 41, 52 and 53. What did the illustrator show that you missed?

questions: Which exaggerating word from the passages is your favourite?
Why does too much description make writing worse?
slides.connect: We found how adjectives and adverbial phrases, used carefully, build vivid settings.

data.locator: Passage 1: Chapter 10, from 'Carefully, Mr Fox began'. Passage 2: Chapter 13, from 'He reached high and'. Passage 3: Chapter 15, from 'Mr Fox laughed and'. About 220 to 240 words each.

synopsis: Passage 1: starving after days underground, Mr Fox tunnels into Boggis's Chicken House.
Passages 2 and 3: he leads his friends to Bunce's Storehouse and Bean's cellar for a great feast.
structure: Mr Fox enters the place carefully
The place and its food are described
The others react with words and actions
Mr Fox takes charge and decides what to take
language: Commands show Mr Fox is the leader; kind names show he loves his family
Adjectives and exaggeration build each setting
Fast, joyful verbs contrast with the slow tunnel verbs

lessons.teacherNotes: Assessment task 3: observe the analysis talk and collect the story maps (EN2-VOCAB-01 building vocabulary; EN2-RECOM-01 using key words to visualise and infer). Copy extracts from your own copy of the book under your school's statutory licence and include the required notice on each copy. The too little and too much examples on the slide are ours, about Farmer Pip's shed, so students can innovate on a sentence from the book without the slide reproducing it.

exitTicket.q: Rewrite with a stronger adjective: There were many hams.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for an exaggerating adjective, e.g. There were hundreds of smoky hams.

exitTicket.q: Write an adverbial phrase that tells where.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a place phrase, e.g. from the rafters, under the floor.

lessons.title: Moral dilemmas
lessons.li: We are learning to discuss a character's moral dilemma and share opinions respectfully.
sc: I can explain a character's dilemma
I can give a reason for my opinion
I can listen to and build on someone else's point

slides.title: Warm-up: Who is who?
slides.prompt: Write quick answers on your whiteboard.
items: Who joins the foxes in Chapter 12?
Whose storehouse do they raid in Chapter 13?
answers: Answers will vary: e.g. loyal, careful, honest, worried

slides.title: Badger has doubts
slides.prompt: Chapter 14 is called Badger Has Doubts. What might he be worried about? Use what you know about the story so far.
slides.notes: Students predict with a partner, then read Chapter 14.

slides.title: Badger and Mr Fox talk
slides.locator: Chapter 14, pp 58 to 60: from 'Suddenly Badger said' to the end of their talk
slides.task: Find what worries Badger and how Mr Fox answers him.
questions: Why does Badger feel doubtful?
How does Mr Fox try to make him feel better?
Do you agree with Mr Fox's reasons? Why?
How does Badger feel at the end?
slides.notes: Add the events of Chapter 14 to the class chart.

slides.title: Mr Fox and Badger
slides.prompt: How are Mr Fox and Badger the same? How are they different?
slides.notes: Add one more idea to each part with the class. Point out that Badger's doubts are what make this a moral dilemma.

slides.means: When a character must choose between two things, and both choices feel partly right and partly wrong.
slides.example: Should Mia tell the teacher her best friend copied, or stay loyal to her friend?

slides.title: Dilemmas in other stories

rows.label: The Lion and the Mouse
rows.text: Should the mouse help the trapped lion, or run to stay safe?

rows.label: Badger
rows.text: Should he take food to save his family, or refuse to steal?

rows.label: You
rows.text: Have you ever had to choose between two hard things?

slides.notes: Students Think-Pair-Share other texts with dilemmas. Then discuss how Badger's choice may clash with his own values.

slides.title: Is it a moral dilemma?

yes.label: Keep a found wallet or hand it in
Tell on a friend or stay quiet
Steal food for a hungry family

no.label: Wear the red or blue shirt

slides.notes: A moral dilemma is about right and wrong. The non-examples are just choices.

slides.title: Conscience alley protocols
points: We share one point at a time
We listen to every speaker
We respect opinions that differ from ours

lessons.li: We are learning how authors build tension and how to add tension to our own writing.
sc: I can find where a story reaches its climax
I can name the small steps and words that build tension

slides.title: Warm-up: Sentence types
slides.prompt: Write: simple statement, exclamation or compound sentence.
items: Rat squeaked, but Mr Fox smiled.

slides.title: Predict
slides.prompt: At the end of Chapter 15, things become risky. Who might appear? What role could this new character play?
slides.notes: Then read Chapter 16 and add it to the class chart.

slides.title: Narrative arc (Freytag's pyramid)
slides.notes: Trace the line with your finger. Tension rises to the climax at the top, then falls. Ask: where are we in Fantastic Mr Fox right now?

slides.means: The most exciting or tense point of a story, just before things start to settle.

slides.title: Tension tools

rows.label: Small steps
rows.text: Each action gets its own short sentence.

rows.label: Strong verbs
rows.text: [verb:froze] is stronger than stopped. [verb:thudded] is stronger than walked.

rows.label: Adverbial phrases

rows.label: Senses

slides.notes: Revise how adverbial phrases add detail about how, when and where, and make the description richer.

slides.title: Does it build tension?
slides.notes: Tension comes from danger getting closer. The non-examples are calm facts.

slides.title: I do: someone is coming
slides.intro: Watch me add tension to my Pumpkin Shed scene.

parts.label: Warning
parts.text: [adv:Suddenly], the latch rattled! Badger froze with a pear in his paw.

parts.label: Closer
parts.text: A yellow circle of lantern light [verb:swept] [adv:across the shelves]. Someone was humming.

parts.label: Hide
parts.text: Mr Fox and the Small Foxes [verb:dived] [adv:into an empty pumpkin crate]. Badger squashed himself [adv:under the bench].

parts.label: Who is it?
parts.text: It was Farmer Pip in her dressing gown, and Biscuit was trotting [adv:beside her].

parts.label: Closer still
parts.text: Biscuit's nose [verb:twitched]. She padded [adv:straight towards the crate].

slides.title: Which builds the most tension?
slides.question: Which sentence builds the most tension?
options: Pip came in and it was night.
why: One quick action, no detail to slow it down.
Extra detail, but nothing gets closer or more dangerous.
Right. A precise verb, and the danger keeps getting closer.
A character fact, not part of the action.

teach.text: An exclamatory sentence shows strong feeling and ends with !. A compound sentence joins two ideas with and, but or so.

items.q: Add . or ! to each.

parts.q: The shed has a red door

items.q: Pick the best joining word: and, but or so.

parts.q: The fox was hungry, ___ he crept to the farm.
Pip set the trap, ___ the fox got away.
Badger dug fast, ___ the cubs helped.

items.q: Write an exclamation a fox might say when he finds food.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for an exclamation mark, e.g. What a feast!

items.q: Is it a statement or an exclamation? What a fright you gave me!
items.answer: An exclamation

items.q: Fix the sentence: how dark it is in here
items.answer: How dark it is in here!

items.q: Join with and: The door opened. Pip walked in.
items.answer: The door opened, and Pip walked in. (or: The door opened and Pip walked in.)

teach.text: and adds an idea. but shows a contrast. so shows a result. Put a comma before but and so.

items.q: Join with and, but or so. Use a comma.

parts.q: The door creaked. The animals hid.
parts.answer: The door creaked, so the animals hid.

parts.q: Pip searched the shed. She found nothing.
parts.answer: Pip searched the shed, but she found nothing.
Biscuit barked, so Pip came running. (and is also acceptable)

items.q: Rewrite as an exclamatory sentence: The shed is very full.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. How full the shed is! or What a full shed!

items.q: Write statement, question or exclamation.

parts.q: How dark it is in here!

items.q: Fix the sentence: the fox ran but biscuit was faster
items.answer: The fox ran, but Biscuit was faster.

items.q: Expand into a compound sentence using so: The tunnel flooded.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. The tunnel flooded, so the animals climbed higher.

items.q: Write a compound sentence about a fox and a farmer using but.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for two complete ideas joined by a comma and but.

teach.text: Exclamations work best when used rarely, at the most exciting moments. A compound sentence can drop a repeated subject: He froze and listened.

items.q: Which is NOT a compound sentence? A: The fox ran, but Pip chased him. B: The fox ran into the dark wood. C: It rained, so they stayed in.
items.answer: B

items.q: Fix the punctuation: what a mess this is said Pip
items.answer: 'What a mess this is!' said Pip.

items.q: Write a tension sentence that ends with an exclamation mark.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. The lantern swung towards them!

items.q: Rewrite with fewer exclamation marks so the important one stands out: We ran! It was dark! Pip was coming! We hid!
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. We ran. It was dark. Pip was coming. We hid!

items.q: Join three ideas in one sentence: Pip stopped. She listened. She walked on.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. Pip stopped and listened, but she walked on.

items.q: Write 3 sentences for a scary moment: one statement, one compound, one exclamation.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for one of each type, correctly punctuated.

exclamatory sentences for strong feelings
adverbial phrases for when, where, how or why
adjectives that build the picture

slides.title: I do: the danger leaves
slides.intro: Watch me finish my Pumpkin Shed scene.

parts.label: Danger closer
parts.text: Biscuit sniffed the crate [adv:from end to end]. A low growl rumbled [adv:in her throat].

parts.label: Animals react
parts.text: [adv:Inside the crate], the Smallest Fox squeezed his eyes shut. Nobody moved a whisker.

parts.label: Dialogue
parts.text: 'Probably just a possum,' yawned Pip. She tapped the lid [adv:with the lantern].

parts.label: Near miss
parts.text: The lid wobbled. A pumpkin rolled off the top and thumped [adv:onto the floor]!

parts.label: Distraction

parts.label: Safe

slides.title: Which sentence shows the danger has gone?
slides.question: Which sentence shows the danger has gone?
why: Pip is still in the shed, so the danger is close.
This raises the tension.
Right. Fainter barking tells us Biscuit and Pip are moving away.
This shows fear. The danger is still there.

rows.label: Satisfy
rows.text: It answers the reader's big question.

rows.label: Complete
rows.text: It makes the story feel whole.

slides.title: Types of resolution (1)

rows.label: Lesson or moral
rows.text: A character learns something important.

rows.label: Surprise
rows.text: The story takes a twist we did not expect.

rows.label: Happy
rows.text: The problem is solved in a good way.

slides.notes: Brainstorm a story the class knows for each type.

rows.label: Funny
rows.text: It ends with a joke or a silly moment.

rows.label: Cliffhanger
rows.text: The problem is not solved, so we are left wondering.

rows.label: Circular
rows.text: The story ends where it began.

slides.title: Which type?
slides.question: The slow tortoise beats the hare, who stopped for a nap. What type of ending is this mainly?
why: The problem is solved: the race is over.
Right. The ending teaches that slow and steady wins.
It does not end where it began.
Every story has some kind of ending.

slides.title: Sort the endings
slides.prompt: What type of resolution is each ending? Drag it.
cards: The lost puppy finds its way home.
The friends win the cup together.
The boy who lied is not believed.
The greedy dog drops his bone.
The door creaks open. The end.
A shadow moves. To be continued.
The leaf lands under its old tree.
Back in bed, just like the start.

Happy: The lost puppy finds its way home.
The friends win the cup together.
Lesson or moral: The boy who lied is not believed.
The greedy dog drops his bone.
Cliffhanger: The door creaks open. The end.
A shadow moves. To be continued.
Circular: The leaf lands under its old tree.
Back in bed, just like the start.

slides.notes: Model one card, then students come up in pairs. Some endings can be two types. Accept a second type if the student explains it.

slides.title: Activity: Sort the endings
steps: Read or recall each picture book.
Decide its type of resolution.
Some books fit more than one type!
Record on the Resolution types poster.
slides.notes: Draw out that many books fit more than one type, such as a funny ending that also teaches a lesson.

slides.title: Walk and talk
slides.prompt: With a partner, walk and talk: what type of resolution do you think Fantastic Mr Fox will have? Why?
slides.notes: Pairs agree on one answer and share with another pair. Then read Chapter 17.

slides.title: Mr Fox's big speech
slides.locator: Chapter 17, pp 79 to 80: from 'But now, my friends' to the cheering
slides.task: In groups, each person plays a character and acts out the scene. Show their feelings.
questions: How do the animals feel about Mr Fox's plan?
What does the cheering tell us?
How does this scene help to wrap up the story?
slides.notes: Groups take parts such as Mr Fox, Badger and the Rabbits. After each performance, use the questions to go deeper.

slides.title: Then...

rows.label: Then
rows.text: Write the Then row of our class chart for Chapter 17.

rows.label: Everyone?
rows.text: Is the problem solved for every character? What about the farmers?

rows.label: Chapter 18
rows.text: Read the last chapter. Then vote: what type of ending is it?

slides.notes: Finally complete the class chart. Read Chapter 18, take a class vote and make a quick graph of the results.

slides.title: Two kinds of happy ending
slides.prompt: Compare the ending of Fantastic Mr Fox with a fairy tale ending.
slides.notes: Use a fairy tale the class knows well, such as Cinderella or Jack and the Beanstalk. Add one more idea to each side, such as the funny last image of the farmers.

slides.support: Name one type of ending for Fantastic Mr Fox and give one reason.
slides.core: Choose a type of ending and justify it with two details from the text.
slides.extend: Argue that it fits two types, with evidence for each.

slides.title: Show me: name the type
slides.prompt: Write the type of resolution.
questions: They solve the problem and have a party.
We never find out if the door opens.
It ends at the same tree where it started.
The bully learns to be kind.
Is the problem solved for every character in Fantastic Mr Fox?
Which type of ending do you enjoy most as a reader? Why?
slides.connect: We learned why stories need a resolution and named six types of endings.

types.name: Surprise
types.means: The story takes a twist we did not expect.

types.name: Happy
types.means: The problem is solved in a good, satisfying way.

types.name: Funny
types.means: It ends with a joke or a silly moment.

types.name: Cliffhanger
types.means: The problem is not solved, so we are left wondering.

types.name: Circular
types.means: The story ends where it began.

lessons.teacherNotes: The Then row of the class chart is finally completed in this lesson, after Chapter 17. Australian picture books such as Pig the Pug, Wombat Stew and Possum Magic work well for the sort, and students may know them already. The vote on Chapter 18 has no single right answer: listen for justification. Many students argue it is both happy and funny, because the farmers are left still waiting.

exitTicket.q: What is the job of a resolution?
exitTicket.answer: To solve or wrap up the problem so the story feels finished.

exitTicket.q: What type of ending does Fantastic Mr Fox have? Give a reason.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. happy, because the animals have food forever; or funny, because the farmers are still waiting.

lessons.title: Planning a narrative
lessons.li: We are learning to plan a narrative sequel with an orientation, complication and resolution.
sc: I can choose an event that causes a new problem
I can plan an orientation, a series of events and a resolution
I can explain my plan clearly to a partner
materials: Narrative arc planner (Freytag's pyramid), one each, plus one enlarged

slides.title: Warm-up: Story parts
slides.prompt: Write quick answers on your whiteboard.
items: What drives the middle of a story?
answers: Characters, setting, time and a hint of a problem
The complication and a series of events
Any two of: lesson, surprise, happy, funny, cliffhanger, circular
The most tense moment of the story

slides.title: Will it last?
slides.prompt: Is Mr Fox's underground plan a forever plan? What could go wrong for the animals?

slides.means: A new story that carries on from an earlier one, with some of the same characters.
slides.example: In our sequel, the animals need a new storehouse when rain floods the tunnels.

slides.title: Is it a good sequel idea?

yes.label: The tunnels flood and the food runs out
A new farmer moves in next door

no.label: Mr Fox has a nice day
The same story again, word for word
A story about a car with no foxes

slides.notes: A sequel needs the same world and characters, and a new problem.

slides.title: Our success criteria
slides.stem: I can plan and write a narrative that includes:
points: an orientation, a complication with a series of events, and a resolution
declarative, exclamatory, simple and compound sentences
adjectives that build descriptions
adverbial phrases for when, where, how or why
slides.notes: Co-construct these from what students know about Fantastic Mr Fox. These criteria are used in every lesson in Week 5.

slides.title: Brainstorm
slides.prompt: What event could stop the animals getting to the farmers' storehouses?
slides.notes: Record ideas on the board: tunnels cave in, a storm floods them, the farmers line their floors with metal, a new guard dog arrives.

slides.title: Characters for our sequel
slides.notes: A strong plot comes from characters who want different things. Fill Biscuit with the class, then ask students to invent one new character of their own.

slides.title: I do: my sequel plan
slides.intro: Watch me plan using the narrative arc.

parts.label: Orientation
parts.text: Months later, the animals feast every night [adv:in the underground village]. Dark clouds roll in.

parts.label: Problem
parts.text: It rains for seven days. The tunnels to the three farms flood.

parts.label: Try 1
parts.text: They dig a new tunnel to Bean's cellar, but they hit solid rock.

parts.label: Try 2
parts.text: The Smallest Fox tries to swim through, but the water is too deep and icy.

parts.label: Climax
parts.text: They dig uphill to Farmer Pip's Pumpkin Shed again, but now Biscuit sleeps inside it!

parts.label: Resolution
parts.text: Mr Fox makes friends with Biscuit. Pip keeps counting her pumpkins and never works out why some are missing.

slides.notes: Fill in the enlarged arc planner as you talk. Name the resolution type: happy and funny.

slides.title: Use the arc planner

stages.label: Orientation
stages.text: A feast in the underground village

slides.notes: Where does each part of my plan go? I have done the first three. Rising action is 2 or 3 tries that fail. The climax is the most tense moment. Ask the class to place the rest of my plan: Biscuit asleep in the Pumpkin Shed, making friends with Biscuit, Pip still counting pumpkins.

slides.title: Activity: Plan your sequel
steps: Choose your problem event.
Fill in the arc planner.
Pick your type of resolution.
Tell your plan to a partner.
slides.notes: Students may plan and write in pairs or alone.

slides.support: Plan with me in a small group. We will fill in the planner together.
slides.core: Complete the arc planner with 2 or 3 tries that fail.
slides.extend: Plan a twist at the climax and a resolution that fits two types.

slides.title: Partner check
slides.prompt: Tell your plan. Partner: listen, then ask one question. Does the action build? Is the problem solved? Does it make sense?
slides.notes: Partners acknowledge ideas and ask questions to clarify. Students then change their plan if needed.

questions: What did your partner's question make you change?
Which part of your plan are you most excited to write?
slides.connect: We planned a sequel with an orientation, a series of events and a resolution.

lessons.teacherNotes: Assessment task 6: collect the arc planners and observe the partner talk (EN2-CWT-01: orientation, complication, resolution structure; EN2-UARL-01: how narratives set up expectations with familiar characters and situations). The model sequel is ours: rain floods the tunnels, and the animals dig uphill to Farmer Pip's Pumpkin Shed, where Pip has left her kelpie Biscuit on guard since their last visit, and Biscuit nearly gives them away. Keep the enlarged plan for Lessons 17 to 19.

exitTicket.q: What problem starts your sequel?
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for an event that blocks the animals' food, e.g. a flood or a locked storehouse.

exitTicket.q: What type of resolution will you use?
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a named type (happy, surprise, funny, lesson, cliffhanger, circular).

reallife.title: A wood on a hill in the rain

items.caption: A wet wood on a hill. Our model sequel begins with rain over a place like this.

reallife.question: What words would help a reader feel this setting?

lessons.li: We are learning to plan and draft an orientation for our narrative sequel.
sc: I can plan characters, setting, time and a hint of the problem
I can write an orientation that draws the reader in
I can revise my orientation with a partner

slides.title: Warm-up: Our sequel plans
slides.prompt: Write quick answers on your whiteboard.
items: What type of resolution will you use?
answers: Answers will vary: an event that blocks the food
Answers will vary: e.g. Mr Fox
Answers will vary: a named type

slides.title: Our class sequel so far

steps.label: Orientation
steps.text: A feast in the underground village

steps.label: Climax
steps.text: Biscuit wakes in the Pumpkin Shed

slides.notes: Today we write the first box. Students check their own plan has a box for each step.

slides.title: What an orientation does
points: Introduces the main and supporting characters
Describes the setting
Tells when it happens
Hints at a problem
Uses engaging details to hook the reader
slides.notes: Recall Lesson 1 and the orientation of Fantastic Mr Fox.

slides.title: How the book opens
slides.locator: Chapter 1, p 1: from 'Down in the valley'
slides.task: Reread the first page. What does the author tell us first?
questions: What do we learn first: place, time or characters?
How does the author make us want to read on?
What hint of trouble is there?
slides.notes: Students notice that the setting comes first, then the characters.

slides.title: I do: plan my orientation
slides.intro: Watch me fill in the Orientation planner.

parts.label: Characters
parts.text: Mr Fox, Badger, the Smallest Fox, Farmer Pip and her kelpie Biscuit

parts.label: Setting
parts.text: the underground village below the hill, and Bluegum Creek Farm over the hill

parts.label: Time

slides.title: I do: my orientation
slides.intro: Watch me turn my plan into an orientation.

parts.label: Time and setting
parts.text: [adv:Many months later], [adv:deep under the hill], the underground village was warm and busy.

parts.label: Characters
parts.text: [adv:Every night], Mr Fox, Badger and all their families shared a [adj:huge], [adj:noisy] feast.

parts.label: More setting
parts.text: The tunnels to the three farms were [adj:wide] and [adj:dry]. Up above, the farmers still sat by the hole, [adj:cold] and [adj:grumpy].

parts.label: New character
parts.text: [adv:Over the hill at Bluegum Creek Farm], Farmer Pip was counting her pumpkins again.

parts.label: Hook
parts.text: Mr Fox smiled. Nothing could go wrong now!

parts.label: Hint
parts.text: But that night, dark clouds [verb:rolled] [adv:over the valley], and it began to rain.

slides.notes: Display this orientation for the rest of the week. Check it against the Lesson 16 success criteria with the class.

slides.title: Show me: which feature?
slides.prompt: Write characters, setting, time or hint of a problem.
questions: Many months later
deep under the hill
Mr Fox, Badger and their families
it began to rain

slides.title: Sort the orientation parts
slides.prompt: Drag each phrase to the part of the orientation it gives us.
slides.notes: Note that One stormy night tells time but also hints at trouble. Accept either if students explain.

slides.title: Which sentence hints at a problem?
slides.question: Which sentence hints at a problem?
why: This shows a feeling, but no trouble yet.
This is setting. Dry tunnels sound safe.
Right. Clouds warn us that rain and trouble are coming.
A happy detail, not a problem.

slides.title: Word bank: opening lines
points: When: [adv:Many months later], [adv:One stormy night], [adv:At the start of winter]
Where: [adv:deep under the hill], [adv:over the hill], [adv:down in the valley]
Hooks: Nothing could go wrong now! / But not for long.
Adjectives: [adj:cosy], [adj:bustling], [adj:gloomy], [adj:peaceful]

slides.title: Our success criteria
slides.stem: I can plan and write a narrative that includes:
points: an orientation, a complication with a series of events, and a resolution

adjectives that build descriptions

slides.notes: These are the criteria from Lesson 16. Today we focus on the orientation.

slides.title: Activity: Plan and draft
steps: Fill in your Orientation planner.
Write your orientation on the writing page.
Read it to a partner.
Revise one thing.

slides.support: Write your orientation with me in a small group, using your plan.
slides.core: Write an orientation with all five features from your planner.
slides.extend: Choose precise adjectives and add one engaging detail that hooks the reader.

slides.title: Peer feedback: Tell, Ask, Give
slides.notes: Partners check for all five orientation features and give one piece of feedback.

questions: Which feature of an orientation was hardest to write?
How does your orientation hint at the problem?
slides.connect: We planned and drafted an orientation that introduces characters, setting and time, and hints at the problem.
slides.notes: Share a few samples, naming the orientation features in each.

prompts.problem: What hint of trouble will I give?
prompts.details: How will I hook the reader?

exitTicket.q: Write the time phrase from your orientation.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a when phrase, e.g. One winter morning.

exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a clue such as a warning, a change in the weather or a strange noise.

lessons.title: Drafting the complication
lessons.li: We are learning to draft a complication and a series of events that build tension.
sc: I can write a problem and two or three tries that fail
I can build tension with small steps, verbs and adverbial phrases
I can revise my events with a partner
materials: class Somebody, Wanted, But, So, Then chart

slides.title: Warm-up: Remember the pattern
slides.prompt: Write quick answers on your whiteboard.
items: Why don't stories solve the problem on the first try?
answers: Failed tries build tension and keep us reading
Answers will vary: small steps, strong verbs, sounds, short sentences

slides.title: How the book did it
slides.prompt: Each failure made the problem worse. Our turn: two or three tries that fail, then a climax.
slides.notes: Read the chain aloud. Ask: how does each step make things worse for the foxes?

slides.title: We do: the problem
slides.intro: Let's write the problem together.

parts.label: Time passes
parts.text: It rained [adv:for seven days and seven nights].

parts.label: News
parts.text: [adv:On the eighth morning], Badger burst [adv:into the dining hall]. 'The tunnels are flooding!' he cried.

parts.label: The problem
parts.text: Muddy water was gushing [adv:into every passage], and the way to the farms was gone.

slides.notes: Write this as an interactive session: students suggest verbs and adverbial phrases.

slides.title: We do: tries that fail
slides.intro: Now the tries. Each one fails.

parts.label: Calm leader
parts.text: Mr Fox did not panic. 'We will dig a new tunnel to Bean's cellar,' he said.

parts.label: Try 1
parts.text: They dug [adv:all morning], but they hit a wall of [adj:solid] rock.

parts.label: Try 2
parts.text: Next, the Smallest Fox tried to swim [adv:through the flooded tunnel], but the water was far too [adj:deep] and [adj:icy].

parts.label: Worse
parts.text: [adv:By the third day], the storerooms were empty. Everyone was hungry again.

slides.notes: Point out the compound sentences with but: each one is a So and a But.

slides.title: We do: the climax
slides.intro: Now we build to the most tense moment.

parts.label: An idea
parts.text: Then Mr Fox remembered the Pumpkin Shed over the hill, high and dry. But since their last visit, Pip had left Biscuit on guard inside.

parts.label: Action
parts.text: 'Get your shovels!' he shouted. They dug uphill [adv:all night].

parts.label: Slow steps
parts.text: [adv:At last], Mr Fox pushed up a floorboard, [adv:very slowly]. Biscuit was asleep [adv:by the door].

parts.label: Cliff edge
parts.text: Her ear [verb:twitched]. Her eyes [verb:opened].

slides.notes: Stop at the climax. The resolution comes tomorrow.

slides.title: How does the tension build?
slides.prompt: Find the success criteria in our writing. Where does the tension get higher? Which sentence is the most tense?

slides.title: Order our series of events
slides.prompt: Drag our class events into order. Where is the most tense moment?
items: It rains for seven days and seven nights.
Badger cries that the tunnels are flooding.
They dig towards Bean's cellar, but hit rock.
The Smallest Fox tries to swim, but it is too deep.
They dig uphill to the Pumpkin Shed.
slides.notes: The last strip is the climax. Students check that their own events also build to one tense moment.

slides.title: Show me: but or so?
slides.prompt: Write but or so.
questions: They dug all morning, ___ they hit rock.
The tunnel flooded, ___ they were trapped.
Badger was tired, ___ he kept digging.
The food ran out, ___ everyone was hungry.

slides.title: Word bank: series of events
points: Time connectives: next, after that, by the third day, at last
Problem words: but, however, unfortunately
Fast verbs: [verb:burst], [verb:gushed], [verb:scrambled], [verb:raced]
Tense moments: Her ear twitched. Nobody moved.

slides.title: Activity: Draft your events
steps: Reread your orientation and plan.
Write the problem.
Write 2 or 3 tries that fail.
Build to your climax.

slides.support: Write the problem and one failed try with me in a small group, or use talk-to-text.
slides.core: Write the problem, 2 or 3 failed tries and the climax over several paragraphs.
slides.extend: Use different sentence types and an adverbial phrase in every paragraph.

slides.title: Peer feedback: Tell, Ask, Give
slides.notes: Partners check that the tension rises with each event. Students apply one piece of feedback.

questions: Where does the tension rise most in your story?
What did you change after feedback?
slides.connect: We drafted a complication and a series of events that build tension towards a climax.

adjectives that build descriptions

lessons.teacherNotes: Write the model as an interactive session: students suggest verbs, adjectives and adverbial phrases while you scribe. Our model follows the plan from Lesson 16: the flood, two failed tries, then the dig uphill to Farmer Pip's Pumpkin Shed. Students who find writing hard can use talk-to-text to draft. Share a few samples where tension grows across the events.

exitTicket.q: Write one failed try as a compound sentence with but.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a try and a failure joined by a comma and but.

exitTicket.q: Where is your climax?
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for the most tense moment just before the problem is solved.

lessons.title: Drafting a resolution
lessons.li: We are learning to draft a resolution that wraps up our narrative.
sc: I can choose a type of resolution that fits my story
I can solve or wrap up the problem for each character
I can use a variety of sentences and correct punctuation

slides.title: Warm-up: Types of resolution
slides.prompt: Name the type.
items: The story ends where it began.
We never find out what happens.
It ends with a big joke.

slides.title: Look back
slides.prompt: What type of resolution did Fantastic Mr Fox have? Which type have you planned for your sequel?

rows.label: Solves
rows.text: The main problem is solved, or clearly not solved for a cliffhanger.

rows.label: Wraps up
rows.text: We know what happens to each important character.

rows.label: Feels right
rows.text: It fits the characters and the story so far.

slides.title: What happens to everyone?
headers: At the end of our sequel
slides.notes: A good resolution wraps up each important character. Fill the last two rows with the class, then students make their own list before drafting.

slides.title: We do: the resolution
slides.intro: Let's finish our sequel together.

parts.label: Turning point
parts.text: Biscuit opened her mouth to bark. Mr Fox did not run.

parts.label: Clever move
parts.text: [adv:Instead], he held out the last ham bone [adv:from the storeroom]. Biscuit sniffed it.

parts.label: Change
parts.text: [adv:Slowly], her tail began to wag!

parts.label: Problem solved
parts.text: [adv:From that night on], Biscuit got a bone every week, and she never barked at the foxes again.

parts.label: Everyone
parts.text: The animals ate pumpkin soup and pear pie [adv:all winter long].

parts.label: Final line
parts.text: And every night, Farmer Pip counted her pumpkins and scratched her head, because a few were always missing.

slides.notes: Write as an interactive session. Check it against the success criteria together. Point out the variety of sentences and the capital letters for names.

slides.title: What type of resolution is this?
slides.question: What type of resolution is our model?
why: The problem is solved, so it is not a cliffhanger.
It does not return to the start.
Right. The animals are fed, and Pip's confusion is funny.
Nobody really learns a lesson here.

what a feast it was
pip counted her pumpkins but some were missing
mr fox said thank you biscuit

Write how the problem is solved.

exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a named type that matches the ending they describe.

exitTicket.q: Write the last sentence of your story.
exitTicket.answer: Answers will vary: look for a sentence that wraps up the problem.

lessons.title: Revising and editing
lessons.li: We are learning to revise and edit our narrative so it is ready to share.
sc: I can explain the difference between revising and editing
I can revise my writing for structure, detail and word choice
I can edit my spelling and punctuation

slides.title: Warm-up: Spot the error
slides.prompt: Write each one correctly.
items: farmer pip lived at bluegum creek
the fox had a long bushy tail
answers: Farmer Pip lived at Bluegum Creek.
The fox had a long, bushy tail.

slides.title: Revise or edit?
slides.prompt: Writers like Roald Dahl revised and edited many times before a book was finished.
slides.notes: Revising makes the writing better. Editing makes it correct. We revise first, then edit.

slides.title: Sort the changes
slides.prompt: Is each change revising or editing? Drag it.
cards: add a comma in a list

skills.title: Plurals: add s or change y

rows.label: Free morpheme
rows.text: Can stand alone as a word: tree, beast, farm.

rows.label: Bound morpheme
rows.text: Cannot stand alone. It changes a word: -s, -es, un-, dis-.

rows.label: Together
rows.text: farm + er + s = farmers

skills.title: Suffixes that change meaning

rows.label: -ly
rows.text: beast + ly = beastly: like a beast. equal + ly = equally: in the same way.

rows.label: -y
rows.text: dust + y = dusty: covered in dust. gloom + y = gloomy: full of gloom.

rows.label: -ing
rows.text: disgust + ing = disgusting: causing disgust.

rows.label: -est

rows.text: Every syllable has at least one vowel sound.

rows.label: Rule 2
rows.text: Suffixes like -ing, -ly and -est usually make their own syllable.

rows.label: Independent clause
rows.text: An idea that can stand alone: Mr Fox crept out.

rows.label: Compound sentence
rows.text: Two equal ideas joined: Mr Fox crept out, and he sniffed the air.

rows.label: Drop the repeat
rows.text: If the subject is the same, you can leave it out: Mr Fox crept out and sniffed the air.

slides.title: and, but, so

rows.text: adds an idea: Pip set the string, [conj:and] she hid.

rows.label: but

rows.label: so
rows.text: shows a result: The cans clanged, [conj:so] Biscuit barked.

rows.label: When
rows.text: [adv:At midnight], the fox woke up. [adv:After a long time], he moved.

rows.label: Where
rows.text: The fox hid [adv:behind the shed]. He crept [adv:along the fence].

skills.title: Ways to spell /ay/
skills.li: We are learning the common ways to spell the /ay/ sound.
sc: I can hear the /ay/ sound in a word
I can sort words by how /ay/ is spelt

slides.means: /ay/ is a diphthong: one sound where your mouth slides from one vowel to another.

rows.label: ai
rows.text: fail, wait, tail, rain, paint, snail, train, chain, plain, raise. Usually in the middle of a word.

rows.label: ay

rows.label: ey
rows.text: they, prey, grey, obey, convey, survey, hey. Not many words.

rows.label: a_e

rows.label: a

rows.label: playing

rows.label: mistaken

items.answer: orientation, complication, resolution

items.q: What type of resolution is this? Tilly finds a new paddock of sweet grass and has the best feast of her life.
items.answer: A happy (resolved) ending

items.q: Write one way an author builds tension.
items.answer: Answers will vary: e.g. small steps in short sentences, strong verbs, sounds, a character coming closer.

items.q: Write: simple statement, exclamation or compound sentence.

parts.q: What a mess you have made!
It rained, so the creek rose.

items.q: Join with and, but or so: Tilly was tired. She kept walking.
items.answer: Tilly was tired, but she kept walking.

items.q: Add commas: The fox had a long bushy red tail.
items.answer: The fox had a long, bushy, red tail.

items.q: Add capital letters and punctuation: farmer pip lives at bluegum creek farm
items.answer: Farmer Pip lives at Bluegum Creek Farm.

items.q: Add speech marks: Over here! called Badger.
items.answer: 'Over here!' called Badger.

items.q: Write Q (quantifying), D (descriptive) or C (classifying) for the adjective in capitals.
Write the adverbial phrase and whether it tells when, where, how or why.

parts.q: The cubs hid under the crates.
Pip crept in without a sound.

items.q: Write a stronger action verb for went.

parts.q: The fox went quietly up the tunnel.
parts.answer: Answers will vary: crept, tiptoed or sneaked

parts.q: The dog went quickly after the cat.
parts.answer: Answers will vary: raced, dashed or bolted

items.q: Write the plural.
Add the suffix.
Which is the correct spelling for an animal's tail: tayl, tail or taile?
items.answer: tail

items.q: Which is the correct spelling: valley, vally or vallee?
items.answer: valley

items.q: Read: Max shared his lunch with the new boy and showed him around the school. Name a trait for Max and give evidence.
items.answer: Answers will vary: look for kind, friendly or caring, with evidence that he shared his lunch or showed the new boy around.

rubric.A: Orientation, complication with a series of events and a satisfying resolution are well developed and linked.
rubric.B: Clear orientation, complication with events, and resolution.
rubric.C: Includes an orientation, a complication and a resolution in order.
rubric.D: Some parts are present; the resolution may be missing or rushed.
rubric.E: Ideas are listed with little narrative structure.

rubric.A: Characters are vivid and consistent, with traits shown through actions, words and thoughts.
rubric.B: Characters show clear traits through actions and some dialogue.
rubric.C: Characters are described with some traits.
rubric.D: Characters are named with little description.

rubric.A: Tension builds through well chosen small steps, verbs and changes of pace, then is released effectively.
rubric.B: Tension builds with small steps and strong verbs.
rubric.C: Some tension is created in one event.
rubric.D: Events are told with little tension.

rubric.A: Controls a wide variety of declarative, exclamatory, simple and compound sentences for effect.
rubric.B: Uses a variety of sentence types correctly.
rubric.C: Uses declarative sentences and some compound and exclamatory sentences.
rubric.D: Mostly simple sentences; some run-on sentences.

rubric.A: Precise adjectives and varied adverbial phrases of time, place, manner and reason build vivid pictures.
rubric.B: Uses a range of adjectives and adverbial phrases.
rubric.C: Uses some adjectives and adverbial phrases of time or place.

rubric.A: Accurate capitals, full stops, commas, ! ? and speech marks; taught words spelt correctly.
rubric.B: Mostly accurate punctuation and spelling of taught words.
rubric.C: Capitals and full stops mostly correct; most taught words spelt correctly.
rubric.D: Punctuation is inconsistent; frequent errors in taught words.
rubric.E: Little control of punctuation and spelling.

Teach the feature with colour-coded examples and non-examples.

Think aloud as you write the model, then write the next part together.
